#7741. If You See Cyan Lights on a Car, Here’s What They Mean

Cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars. Here's what the unusual color means and why federal regulators want to standardize it.

Colored lights play an important part in driving safety. Red brake lights mean a vehicle is slowing down, amber turn signals indicate someone is turning, flashing red and blue indicate an emergency, and yellow lights can mean a hazard or warning.

But what about cyan? Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed new federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.

Learn what the color would mean, where it’s already appearing, and what drivers should expect in the future.

Cyan lights would indicate that a vehicle’s automated driving system is in control and no one inside needs to actively monitor the road. The lights could appear on cars with someone behind the wheel or vehicles that operate without a human driver.

On Oct. 23, NHTSA announced a proposal to establish federal standards for these lights, including their placement and brightness. The lights would remain steady rather than flash, and drivers would be able to see them from all sides of the vehicle. The proposal is part of a broader effort to update safety requirements for automated vehicles, including those NHTSA describes as “vehicles designed never to be driven by a human being.”

“As automotive technology continues to evolve, our safety standards must keep pace with innovation in ways that do not compromise public safety,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in the agency’s release. “These proposed updates address unnecessary regulatory burdens for vehicles built without traditional manual controls while establishing clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps. By aligning our regulations with today’s technology, we are paving the way for safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”

Cyan would help other drivers, pedestrians, and law enforcement recognize when an automated system is handling the driving. Unlike common driver-assistance features that help with steering or speed, these systems can operate without constant human supervision under certain conditions.

The lights wouldn’t give self-driving cars any special privileges or change how other drivers should behave around them.

Mercedes-Benz has already received permission to use turquoise-colored lights on certain vehicles in California and Nevada. California approved testing on freeways, while Nevada allowed the lights on certain production vehicles.

The lights work with Mercedes-Benz’s Drive Pilot system, which can handle driving under specific conditions. A driver still needs to remain available to take control when requested. The company has tested the lights near the outside mirrors and on the front and rear of its vehicles.

“Mercedes-Benz is committed to standardizing the color turquoise,” the company said in a release, explaining that the goal is to make automated driving systems easier for people to recognize around the world.

Those approvals came before NHTSA’s latest proposal, which could establish a consistent standard for other manufacturers across the country. For now, the new federal rules are still under consideration. Even if NHTSA finalizes them, carmakers wouldn’t have to install cyan lights on self-driving vehicles. Manufacturers that choose to use them would need to follow the new standards.

Under the proposal, the lights could turn on when the automated system is driving without someone monitoring the road. They’d have to turn off when a person is expected to resume that responsibility. Drivers wouldn’t need to do anything differently when they see cyan lights, but they’d have a clearer idea of who’s controlling the vehicle.

National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, “Trump’s Transportation Department Makes Commonsense Updates to Vehicle Lighting Standards for AVs”

#7740. Arkansas Bar Official Allegedly Transferred Points from Some Bar Examinees to Others

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From the Arkansas Supreme Court Thursday:

Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.

An internal review by Robert Brech, Executive Director of the Supreme Court of Arkansas's Office of Professional Conduct and Programs, has uncovered extensive irregularities involving the Court's Office of Professional Programs and the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination. The matter was turned over to state and federal authorities.

As of today, the Prosecuting Attorney's Office for the Sixth Judicial District filed formal criminal charges against Nancie Givens for 65 counts of tampering with a public record under Arkansas Code Annotated section 5-54-121 in connection with the alleged altering of numerous Arkansas Bar Examination scores and the deletion of files purportedly intended to conceal that misconduct. The charges followed a criminal investigation initiated in April 2026 by the Arkansas State Police and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. As always, all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

Moving forward, we are committed to holding those involved accountable, taking continued corrective oversight of the Arkansas Bar Examination, and determining the appropriate course of action.

In February 2026, Givens, the former Executive Director of this Court's Office of Professional Programs, resigned. At that time, Robert Brech was serving as Executive Director of the Court's Office of Professional Conduct. Following Givens's resignation, the Court directed Brech to supervise the Office of Professional Programs, which oversees the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination.

Upon his review of the Office of Professional Programs' records and administrative operations, Brech discovered that a large number of files and electronic communications were modified or deleted in early January 2026. Approximately 11,400 files were deleted or rendered unavailable. Most of those files included Arkansas Bar examinee applications, profiles, and examination score sheets that the Office of Professional Programs was required by this Court's rules to retain for twenty-five years.

Brech immediately notified a member of this Court, who directed him to determine the extent of the missing records and identify any other irregularities. On the basis of his review of the remaining files, Brech identified numerous discrepancies involving Arkansas Bar Examination scores across at least eight test administrations between July 2020 and July 2025. At that time, the matter was referred to the appropriate state and federal authorities.

Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.

The vast majority of examinees who were previously informed that they had passed the Arkansas Bar Examination by the Office of Professional Programs did, in fact, pass the exam. Those examinees affected will be notified by the Office of Professional Conduct as soon as possible upon definitive confirmation of their status.

The Court is working with state and federal authorities to recover deleted and missing data, analyze all test administrations within that time frame, and determine the full scope of this grave and potentially criminal abuse of power. The people of Arkansas deserve, and the Court is committed to providing, total transparency in this matter. However, further disclosure will be forthcoming in a manner so as to not compromise the ongoing state and federal criminal investigations. Accordingly, additional disclosures will be limited as those efforts remain underway.

As an immediate step, independent of any state or federal criminal investigation or prosecution, Nancie Givens has been referred to the Office of Professional Conduct for investigation of extensive violations of the Arkansas Rules of Professional Conduct. See Ark. R. Prof. Conduct 8.1(a) & 8.4(a)-(e). Furthermore, new testing procedures and security measures were implemented with the February 2026 administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination to ensure systemic accountability and safeguard the integrity of the examination.

We recognize the profound consequences for affected examinees, the Bar, and the public at large. Our paramount concern is safeguarding litigants, the integrity of the legal profession, and public confidence in the administration of justice. While these matters remain under criminal and administrative investigation, we commit to pursue continued corrective measures in an effort to reestablish confidence in our institution.

My family spends a lot of time on our deck, and even when fall evenings start getting chilly, we still find ourselves wanting to be out there. To extend our outdoor living window, we’ve traditionally kept a basket of blankets available by the door and a stack of wood ready by the fire pit. But since building a fire isn’t always convenient, and huddling under a throw isn’t always sufficient, it’s not long before we’re back inside—enjoying our gas fireplace and worrying about the added energy cost only after the bill arrives.

Once we got it set up, Timber Stoves’ Scout tabletop pellet heater provided the perfect solution to our cold-weather woes. After spending many an evening over the last month enjoying eye-level fires that start in just a few seconds, here’s what we love about the unit and what you deserve a warning on before you buy your own.

Bottom line: The Timber Stoves Scout is a stylish, effective solution for outdoor warmth, offering ease of use and maintenance despite initial setup challenges.

Before we started testing the Scout, we definitely had our reservations. In a home with two high-energy dogs and a revolving door of teenagers, was it even safe to have a wood pellet stove on our picnic table? Then there was assembly, which was challenging at first. The instructions weren’t super clear, so we struggled to get the chimney to fit over the main chamber. We ended up using a flat-head screwdriver to nudge open the gap that runs the length of the chimney, and that provided the fraction of an inch it needed to slide on. We also weren’t sure whether to insert the self-tapping screws to keep everything connected (the instructions said yes, but an online video we found implied no—we went with yes). Even getting the pellets to light took a few tries, but once we added a couple of small pieces off some GreenSpark fire starters we had, they took right off.

The good news is that once we got that first fire lit, our worries were a thing of the past. The Scout has an absolutely charming aesthetic, and we quickly fell in love with its functionality as well. The viewing window is perfect for watching your own tiny fire while you share a meal or play a game, and once it’s cranking, it puts out impressive warmth over about a 5-foot radius. We actually got too hot the first night we used it (early evening temps were still in the low 60s), but all we had to do was stop adding pellets from the hopper, and it slowly died down on its own.

Beyond its impressive heat, the Scout tabletop pellet heater features a rugged design that’s clearly built to last. While we weren’t sure it would be safe to have a tall wood pellet stove up off the ground, the weighted base has kept it rock-solid and stable no matter how many times our dogs have crashed into the table. I definitely wouldn’t leave small children unsupervised around an appliance like this, but that’s standard for any fireplace or fire pit.

Upkeep has been a pleasant surprise as well. The dedicated ash collection tray makes cleanup quick and easy—you just dump the cooled ash between uses to keep air flowing freely through the chamber and add fresh pellets to the hopper. After enjoying at least a dozen fires over the past few weeks, the stainless steel body has taken on a pretty purple-and-brown patina in many places, and I’ve simply wiped off any soot that’s collected inside the viewing window with a dry paper towel. All this to say, if I had to assemble it all over again to get to where I am today, I’d do it in a heartbeat.

#7736. Lindsay Clancy judge considers retrial at hearing to dismiss murder case

Lindsay Clancy was being tried for first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children and claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis. (Photo by CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via the Associated Press)

The possible retrial date for Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with strangling and killing her three small children in 2023, might be March 2027, according to a Massachusetts judge during a Monday hearing to determine whether the triple murder case should be dismissed.

Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan offered the tentative retrial date, and prosecutors in the case said they fully intend to retry Clancy, 36, who admitted to strangling to death her three children—5-year-old daughter Cora; 3-year-old son Dawson; and 8-month-old son Callan—during a postpartum psychosis episode. She later cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window, which paralyzed her from the waist down, according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

The five-week trial resulted in a jury deadlock after one juror held out to convict Clancy. Eleven jurors were prepared to present a not guilty by reason of insanity verdict, which would have sent Clancy to a psychiatric facility instead of sentencing her to life in prison.

Michael Desronvil, the lone dissenter, wanted to convict and faced scrutiny after his name was leaked on the internet.

Jennifer Sprague, a Plymouth County, Massachusetts, assistant district attorney, defended Desronvil’s decision but did not comment on what charges that Clancy would face in a new trial.

From collapsible, fold-flat Christmas trees and re-plantable living trees to accents straight from your backyard or the grocery store, there are plenty of clever ways to celebrate big without cluttering your home.

One way to save space after the holiday is to plant your tree in your own backyard. By choosing a living Christmas tree, you’ll save space, reduce waste, and build memories that last for years to come. A living Christmas tree is sold with its roots still attached, often called a “balled and burlapped” tree. Not only will a living tree fill your home with a fresh pine scent, but replanting it provides environmental benefits, such as minimizing waste, reducing deforestation, providing wildlife habitat, and sequestering carbon. You’ll be able to extend your holiday joy by incorporating replanting the tree as part of your celebration with friends and family, and you’ll be able to enjoy it throughout the year. Look for a living Christmas tree at nurseries, garden centers, online retailers like Lynch Creek Farm and Trees.com, and specialized tree farms.

You can also look for inflatables like trees, gift boxes, and snowmen that can be used inside or outside. Once deflated, they’ll be easier to store.

#7734. Prosecution Over Threat to American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten Can Go Forward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From U.S. v. Spitzer (N.D. Ga.), filed by Magistrate Judge John Larkins on Oct. 9, and just affirmed Wednesday by Judge Eleanor Ross:

The indictment alleges that on July 23, 2024, Mr. Spitzer posted the following message on the website for the American Federation of Teachers, a labor union, regarding its president ("Individual #1"):

[Individual #1] is an ignorant incompetent cunt that should be worried for her safety. Fact that she is still alive. Liberal nazi deserves the bullet to head. Resign before she ends like what happened to trump at his speech. They won't miss fat bitch.

The indictment alleges that the post violated 18 U.S.C. § 875(c), which makes it a federal crime to transmit in interstate commerce any communication containing a threat to injure another person.

Mr. Spitzer argues that assuming the allegations in the indictment were true, it fails to state an offense because the posting was not a "true threat," or even a threat at all, and thus is protected by the First Amendment. As he sees it, the posting was simply political speech about a public figure and did not advocate the use of force or violence against Individual #1.

{In an effort to contextualize the posting, Mr. Spitzer points to an internet article in which Mike Pompeo, the former U.S. Secretary of State, described Individual #1 as "the most dangerous person in the world"; examples of "conservative politicians and commentators" criticizing her approach to school closures during the pandemic; and examples of Individual #1's own political statements. But these are not facts that the Court can consider at this juncture because they fall outside the four corners of the indictment.}

The government responds that whether Mr. Spitzer's posting qualified as a true threat is a question for the jury and that a pretrial determination of the sufficiency of the evidence is procedurally improper. The government further asserts that Mr. Spitzer improperly relies on facts not alleged in the indictment to contextualize the posting. The government has the better argument….

Considering the allegations on the face of the indictment—as this Court must—the Court finds that a jury could conclude that Mr. Spitzer's alleged posting constituted a "true threat." There are at least four separate references to harming or killing Individual #1, including: that she should be "worried for her safety"; that she "deserves a bullet to [the] head"; that unless she resigns she risks being shot similar to the attempted assassination of President Donald J. Trump; and that she will not be missed. In addition, the posting makes an oblique reference to her still being alive, which when combined with the other statements, can reasonably be interpreted as evidencing a present intent to intimidate and place Individual #1 in fear of bodily harm or death. The screed's liberal use of epithets further tends to show that the posting was not simply on a matter of public concern, but rather a threat against Individual #1 personally….

In his reply, Mr. Spitzer relies on the Supreme Court's decision in Watts v. United States, to argue that "political hyperbole" is not a "true threat." True enough, but Watts is distinguishable. In that case, the Supreme Court overturned the conviction of Watts, an 18-year-old Black protester who was charged with threatening President Lyndon B. Johnson during a political rally at the Washington Monument during the 1960's. During the protest, Watts said:

They always holler at us to get an education. And now I have already received my draft classification as 1-A and I have got to report for my physical this Monday coming. I am not going. If they ever make me carry a rifle the first man I want to get in my sights is L.B.J. They are not going to make me kill my black brothers.

The Supreme Court held that considering the full context of the statement—including that it was conditional upon Watt's joining the military (which he said he would not do) and that the listeners laughed at his statement—it was "political hyperbole," not a true threat. In contrast, Mr. Spitzer's alleged statement is much more threatening for the reasons explained above. Also, significantly, Watts was decided after trial, based on a developed evidentiary record, which underscores why dismissal at this juncture is not appropriate.

Accordingly, dismissal of the indictment is not warranted. But, of course, Mr. Spitzer is free to renew his challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence at trial….

Brent A. Gray and Eric John White represent the government.

#7733. That Hole in Your Ruler Isn’t Random – Here’s What It’s Actually For

That small hole on a ruler has a practical purpose and an unexpected history. Here's why it exists and how people use it.

Almost everyone has used a ruler at some point, whether it was for a school project, measuring something around the house, or drawing a straight line. But even after years of using one, there’s a small detail that’s easy to miss: the hole near the end.

Those holes in rulers aren’t just part of the design. They actually serve a purpose, and the reason they’re there goes back further than most people might expect. Here’s what they’re for, how they were used in the past, and a few other ways they come in handy.

The hole at the end of a ruler is mainly there for storage. It lets people hang the ruler on a hook, nail, or pegboard instead of leaving it in a drawer or on a workbench. This is particularly helpful with longer metal rulers that might not fit in a toolbox.

But the hole has been around for much longer than modern workshops. Years ago, before paper notebooks became common in schools, students practiced writing on small slate boards. They could wipe away their writing with a damp cloth and use the board again.

Some students tied that cloth to their rulers with a piece of string through the hole. That way, they always had something nearby to clean their slates. Schools eventually moved away from slate boards, but the holes remained. Today, they’re mostly there to make rulers easier to hang and store.

Hanging a ruler isn’t the only reason manufacturers add holes. Some rulers have several, and they can serve different purposes depending on where they’re placed. For example, certain school rulers have three holes spaced along one side. These line up with the rings in a standard three-ring binder, so students can keep their rulers with their other school supplies.

Some rulers also have holes that help with drawing circles. A pin through one hole can hold the ruler in place while a pencil in another hole traces a circle as the ruler turns. Not every ruler has holes designed for this, but specialty models like the Creative Grids Quick Trim Ruler do. A compass is still a better choice when exact measurements matter.

Some crafting rulers have holes for more specific jobs. Quilting rulers and templates may have openings that help mark circles or line up fabric before cutting. Others have slots or shaped edges that guide a rotary cutter, making it easier to cut certain shapes.

There are also special rulers for paper crafts and stitching. Some have rows of tiny, evenly spaced holes that help people mark where to make stitches or decorative patterns.

Of course, not every ruler has holes. Smaller plastic rulers often don’t need them, while longer metal versions may have one at each end. It mostly comes down to how the manufacturer expects people to use the ruler. And for everyday measuring, the holes don’t make much difference. A ruler without them can measure just as accurately as one with them.

#7730. Winter Storm Watch vs. Winter Storm Warning: What’s the Difference?

A winter storm watch and winter storm warning mean different things. Here's what each alert signals and how to prepare for dangerous weather.

Tracking severe weather can sometimes feel like it requires a degree in meteorology. With complex scientific terms and technical jargon, it can be difficult to understand what it all means and what should be done to prepare. That’s when the difference between a winter storm watch and a winter storm warning matters.

Both alerts come from the National Weather Service, but they call for different levels of urgency. Here’s how the alerts work and what homeowners should do when they see one.

A winter storm watch means a significant winter storm is possible, but forecasters aren’t yet sure where or when it will hit or how severe it will be. According to the National Weather Service, watches often arrive a day or two before a storm and can cover heavy snow, sleet, or ice.

They give residents time to prepare, even though the storm may not reach their area. As the forecast becomes clearer, the National Weather Service may upgrade the watch to a warning, issue an advisory, or cancel it altogether.

A winter storm warning means dangerous winter weather is expected or already happening. Heavy snow, sleet, or ice could make travel unsafe and cause other problems, including power outages. The amount of snow or ice needed to trigger a warning varies by location.

“Each office knows the local area and will issue Warnings, Watches or Advisories based on local criteria,” according to the National Weather Service. “For example, the amount of snow that triggers a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Northern Plains is typically much higher than the amount needed to trigger a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Southeast.”

Warnings generally arrive closer to a storm’s arrival than watches, although forecasters can issue one before snow or ice begins falling.

A winter weather advisory means snow, sleet, or ice is expected to cause problems, but forecasters don’t anticipate conditions severe enough for a warning. An advisory may signal slick roads or other travel disruptions. While the weather may be less severe than during a warning, residents should still take precautions and monitor local forecasts.

A winter storm watch gives homeowners time to prepare before conditions worsen. That includes checking heating systems, protecting exposed pipes from freezing, and stocking up on food, medications, and other essentials.

“Your primary concerns at home or work during a winter storm are loss of heat, power and telephone service and a shortage of supplies if storm conditions continue for more than a day,” according to the National Weather Service.

Homeowners should have flashlights, spare batteries, and a charged phone in case the power goes out. Checking smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, locating snow shovels, and stocking up on ice melt can also help.

Once a warning takes effect, homeowners should finish their preparations and avoid unnecessary travel. Staying indoors is generally safest during severe winter weather.

If the power goes out, residents can close off unused rooms and wear extra layers to stay warm. Portable generators should always remain outdoors, away from windows and doors. Grills and ovens should never serve as heating sources because they can create serious safety hazards.

Residents should continue monitoring weather alerts throughout the storm. Once conditions improve, homeowners can check for damage and begin clearing snow and ice from walkways and driveways.

I wanted to ensure that any window insulation kit we recommended was truly effective and easy to install, so I put each of these kits to the test. It’s worth noting that without a laboratory full of expensive machinery and repeatable, consistent conditions, it’s hard to objectively determine which window insulation kits insulated better. However, all the kits we included on this list were effective at stopping any noticeable air movement or condensation.

There are a number of factors to consider when shopping for window insulation kits. They’re available in different foil types, such as plastic, magnetic, and reflective. Features like film thickness, dimensions, reusability, and installation requirements will determine which insulation kit is most suitable for your home.

Several window insulation product types are on the market: plastic film, magnetic barriers, and reflective foil insulation.

Windows come in all sizes, so look for kits with enough film to cover your windows. Most kits come with enough plastic sheets and double-sided tape to seal several windows. It’s essential for shoppers to know their windows’ dimensions to determine which kit will work for their home.

Window insulation kits create a trap for air between the window and the film. That trap is called an air lock. Double-sided tape, which holds the film in place on the window pane, will create an air lock. By pressing the film firmly onto the tape, users can create a strong bond that keeps drafts out.

To create a long-lasting seal, durable film is a must. Durability is often determined by the film’s thickness. Thick film offers more resistance to punctures from kids or pets. It’s also easier to apply correctly, thus establishing a good seal. Thick film does a better job of insulating windows. Standard window film is about 19 micrometers (μm) thick, while heavy-duty film can be as thick as 38 μm.

Some homes have only one or two truly drafty windows, while others have a slew of them. Choose a kit that has enough film to cover all the drafty windows. Many kits come in multipacks that can cover up to 10 windows. They come with sheets of film that can be cut to size, so every window that needs insulation can be covered.

Window insulation kits are meant to be temporary solutions to drafty windows. The good news is that most of these kits are reusable, so buyers won’t have to purchase a new kit every year. Films 19 μm or thicker can be peeled off the double-sided tape, folded up, and stored when winter is over. The double-sided tape won’t be reusable, but a roll of double-sided tape is cheaper than a houseful of window kits.

The best window insulation kits are effective, affordable, and easy to install. Most kits are installed by placing double-sided tape around the perimeter of the window jamb. Then, window film is applied to the tape. At the bottom of the window, the film is attached to a piece of tape on the sill, making a seal. Finally, the film is heated with a handheld blow dryer to create a transparent, airtight seal free from wrinkles.

Still have questions about choosing the best window insulation kits? Here’s some more information to help you decide.

Window insulation kits create an effective barrier preventing cold air from entering a home. Heat-shrink film applied to the window pane with double-sided tape creates an air gap that works like a thermal window.

Insulated curtains do a good job of keeping the cold temperatures at bay, but they don’t create airtight seals to hold back drafts like window insulation kits do. Plus, insulated curtains must be closed to work, so they block natural light. Window insulation film is usually clear, so it doesn’t block those precious rays of winter sun from shining into a home.

Some window insulation kits claim to reduce a home’s energy consumption by up to 35 percent. Users will need to install these products carefully and on every leaky window to maximize their effectiveness.

#7728. Court Allows Discovery as to Vindictive Prosecution Defense by Smartmatic's Parent Company

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"It may well be that no fire will be discovered under all the smoke, but there is enough smoke here ... to warrant the unusual step of ... find[ing] out how this unusual prosecution came about."

From U.S. v. SGO Corp. Ltd., decided Tuesday by Judge Kathleen Williams (S.D. Fla.):

For a six-year period, the Government investigated SGO executives for their role in a money laundering and bribery scheme related to the May, 2016 Philippine elections. The investigation culminated in a six-count indictment ("First Indictment"), returned on August 8, 2024, which charged [executives of] SGO and Smartmatic … [with] conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act ("FCPA") (Count I); violations of the FCPA (Count II); conspiracy to commit money laundering (Count III); and international laundering of monetary instruments (Counts IV, V, and VI). The FCPA "prohibits officers of a domestic concern from making corrupt payments to a 'foreign official.'"

SGO was not charged. In fact, SGO had been cooperating with the Government since 2021, years before the First Indictment was returned. {Although the Parties may dispute the breadth and quality of SGO's efforts to cooperate, there is no question that SGO and the Government were engaged in discussions and the exchange of documents related to this matter.}

The original trial date was set for October 7, 2024 … [but was eventually reset for 2026]….

As the court notes, the Trump Administration was skeptical of FCPA prosecutions, deprioritized FCPA enforcement generally, and "elected to close FCPA investigations into multiple companies." But despite that, in October 2025, the government added SGO as a defendant in the case. SGO then moved to dismiss the superseding indictment, alleging vindictive and selective prosecution, and sought discovery in support of that motion, "premised on political events that have embroiled Smartmatic in the wake of the 2020 election":

Since that election, multiple high-profile individuals and organizations connected to then-Former President Donald Trump have alleged that Smartmatic, a subsidiary of SGO, interfered in the election…. President Trump has also reposted content blaming Smartmatic for interfering in United States and Venezuelan elections, calling Smartmatic "disgraceful" and expressing that those who "rigged" the 2020 election must pay. In response to the statements by President Trump's confederates, Smartmatic brought various defamation suits, which are largely ongoing. SGO contends that President Trump's personal animus against SGO and assertion of its rights against President Trump's confederates precipitated the filing of the Superseding Indictment….

The court lays out the demanding standard for defendants' attempts to get discovery related to allegations of vindictive or selective prosecution, but concludes that in this case the standard was met. A brief excerpt (for more, including citations to precedents to which the court analogizes this case, see the full opinion):

First, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by evidence that the Government bucked a trend in enforcement activity in prosecuting the defendant…. [W]hile the Blanche and Bondi Memos and Executive Order 14209 explicitly announced an intention to rein in and limit FCPA enforcement, particularly against corporations, SGO was charged, nonetheless.

Second, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by the timing between a defendant's assertion of a right and the allegedly vindictive prosecutorial act…. [Here,] it is telling that the Government chose not to indict SGO originally, that SGO was charged only after President Trump reassumed office and after SGO had been cooperating with the Government for years, and that the Government has presented no evidence adduced between the First and Superseding Indictments warranting SGO's addition as a defendant.

Third, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by the Executive, prosecutor, or law enforcement's stated positions, even when they do not explicitly admit that the case was brought against the defendant for an improper purpose…. The Court finds probative not just that President Trump signed an executive order regarding FCPA enforcement but also that President Trump has personally expressed animus towards SGO regarding election interference. Indeed, President Trump's confederates were sued by SGO for making false claims regarding SGO's role in interfering with the 2020 presidential election that President Trump lost….

After evaluating the totality of the circumstances in this case, the Court has concluded that limited discovery regarding SGO's Motion to Dismiss is warranted…. [T]ere is "some evidence" tending to support SGO's Motion to Dismiss: the individual Defendants were charged over a year prior to when the Superseding Indictment against SGO was returned; for years prior to the initiation of this case and up until the Superseding Indictment was returned, SGO was cooperating with the Government; the Government charged SGO amidst a public shift away from charging defendants for similar FCPA violations; SGO brought suit against the President's confederates prior to being charged; and the President has expressed at least some degree of animus towards SGO. "It may well be that no fire will be discovered under all the smoke, but there is enough smoke here … to warrant the unusual step of … find[ing] out how this unusual prosecution came about."

[T]he Government shall provide the Court with the following for ex parte and in camera review under seal:

NEXT: Prosecution Over Threat to American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten Can Go Forward

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7727. Tool Trials: Putting Ridgid’s Cordless Crown Stapler To the Test

Is a cordless stapler a real upgrade, or just a nice-to-have? I put one to the test to find out.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Last spring, I was sitting at home with my family watching football on a Sunday when my wife caught me doing what I often do: scrolling Zillow. “What don’t you like about the house we’re in?” she asked. I told her that ever since I finished the basement, I’d missed having a shop space to work on projects.

Her answer: “Then build that garage you always wanted.”

Fast forward eight months, and my new garage is up. I’m insulating the main level and sheathing it with OSB before adding cabinets and shelving and moving on to the upstairs. It’s a big garage; we’re talking 30-plus rolls of insulation on the main level, so on a run to pick up the next half-dozen rolls, I wandered down the tool aisle and saw the Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler staring back at me.

Beyond getting the garage insulation up faster, it looked like a tool I’d keep using on future wiring and upholstery projects, and the same goes for anyone re-screening a porch, recovering a chair seat, or tacking down low-voltage wire.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler is a 3-lb. battery-powered stapler that runs on Ridgid’s 18V battery platform. It features an integrated LED light, an onboard wire and screen attachment, a depth adjustment knob, and a belt hook.

It drives 3/8-in. crown (T50) staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long. Ridgid claims it can drive 105 staples per minute and up to 6,800 staples on a single charge of a 4.0 Ah battery.

One last note, and in full transparency, I’m a regular user of Ridgid tools myself: Ridgid offers a lifetime service agreement on its tools as long as you register them within 90 days of purchase.

My goal was to install a half-dozen rolls of insulation, then run wire to an outlet to try out the wire attachment. I wanted to see how easy the tool was to use, whether it jammed, and what I liked and didn’t like about it.

The short version: this tool is awesome. No jams, nothing wonky. It’s as simple as load, point, and pull the trigger. It took a little playing with the depth knob to get the staples seating at the right depth, but I had it figured out within a handful of staples.

I really like the wire attachment. I try to keep my wiring clean and neat, usually with zip ties and tie mounts. With this attachment, running the wire was simple, and the stapler did it much more neatly than I expected.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the onboard LED light. It has its own trigger, separate from the firing trigger, so I could turn it on only when I needed it.

It’s also easy on the battery. I put up six rolls of insulation during the test and a couple more off camera, and the indicator on the 2.0 Ah battery didn’t budge.

There were a couple of things I didn’t like, though they’re minor. First, Ridgid advertises dry-fire lockout on this stapler, which I took to mean it wouldn’t fire once the staples ran out. On mine, it still did. To be fair, it never marred the work surface, which Ridgid lists as one of the lockout’s benefits, so it may be doing part of its job. But it was annoying to pull the trigger and have nothing come out, and it made it easy to miss that I was out of staples.

Second, the depth drifted. After every 20 or 30 staples, I’d notice they were no longer seating at the depth I’d set and were starting to sit proud. I don’t know if that was due to denser 2x4s or inconsistencies between strips of staples, but it was something to keep an eye on. When I noticed it, I’d add a few clicks on the depth knob.

I really like this tool. If you’re only insulating a garage, it’s really nice to have, but not essential. You could get by with a standard stapler. That said, the LED light, the wire attachment, and the price, especially with the battery and charger included, make this a tool I know I’ll use more than I expected on future projects.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The tool alone retails at The Home Depot for $119, but for the last few months, there’s been a special buy that includes the tool, a charger, and a 2.0 Ah Ridgid battery for $104.

Ridgid is owned by Emerson Electric Co., which makes the red Ridgid plumbing and pipe tools directly. The orange Ridgid cordless power tools, including this stapler, are made by Techtronic Industries (TTI), the company behind Milwaukee and Ryobi, under a licensing agreement with Emerson.

No. Staple guns need staples that match the tool’s crown width, leg length, and wire gauge. The Ridgid 18V crown stapler takes 3/8-in. crown staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long, including standard T50 staples. Other staplers may use different types, like narrow-crown or other heavy-duty series, so check the tool or the manual before you buy.

#7726. This Trending Home Feature Is More Practical Than Pretty

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 8, 2026 11:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Each year, Zonda publishes an annual Cost vs. Value (CVV) report, ranking the most common home renovation projects across the nation by return on investment (ROI) value. For the first time, backup power generators entered the top 10 ranking on the list at number 7, with ROI exceeding 100 percent in hurricane-prone and storm-affected regions.

We wanted to understand why home backup power is more popular than ever, since it’s long been considered a luxury upgrade as opposed to an essential part of modern home preparedness. Here’s what several home generator experts and real estate pros think are the reasons why homeowners and homebuyers are now prioritizing backup power and whole-home generators when it comes to home value.

Before we dive into the reasons more people are opting to have a standby generator or whole-home backup generator, it’s important to understand exactly what it does and how it functions. Permanently installed outside a home, a standby generator produces enough electricity to power an entire house indefinitely in the event of a power outage. It connects directly to the home’s electrical panel and uses the natural gas line for fuel. One of the major benefits is that a standby generator automatically turns on within seconds of the power going out, seamlessly transferring the power source from the grid to the generator.

A portable generator is a gas-powered machine that you can carry or wheel over short distances. It has outlets so you can power several appliances. However, it only functions as a temporary power source when the electricity shuts off, making it less reliable than a standby generator. It’s also noisier, requires setup each time you use it, and needs to be refueled periodically.

This whole-home standby generator features a dual-fuel design and a transfer switch that automatically kicks on when the power goes out.

A rise in storm frequency and severity plays a role in more people wanting a backup generator for their home. “Outages stopped feeling rare,” says Beau Tyrrel, product training manager at Jackery. “The average U.S. customer lost about 11 hours of power in 2024, nearly double the decade before. When something happens twice as often, people start planning for it.”

Bert Woidan, operations manager at Trademark Electric, a Generac PowerPro Prestige dealer in Ocala, Florida, recognizes how generator sales are a storm-driven market. “I believe with the increase in weather-related power outages, it only makes sense that more homeowners would want a backup generator with their home,” he explains. “When our company first started selling generators over 20 years ago, I remember standing in the parking lot talking with our founder, and we set a goal to install at least one generator a week. Today, we order generators by the semi load, and during a busy storm season, we’re installing two to three generators a day.”

More storms mean more stress over potential damage. “Especially in our region, if you lose power, the biggest concern is your AC going out,” notes Woidan. “With how humid it gets, it’s not just uncomfortable, but the humidity and moisture can damage your home very quickly, so it’s super important to keep your AC running even if you lose power.”

In the Midwest, the big fear is the basement, says Omar Muhammad, owner of Excel Electrical Technologies in Orland Park, Illinois. “Most homes in our area have a sump pump, and the storms that knock out power are the same storms that send water toward your foundation.” A finished basement can take on tens of thousands of dollars of damage in one night if the pump stops, so buyers and residents understand that a generator protects the most expensive square footage in their house.

Technological innovation has been a game changer for how Americans live. Homes depend on electricity in ways they didn’t 20 years ago, says Muhammad. “A lot of people work from home now and some run medical equipment. Many have an EV in the garage; a high-efficiency furnace that won’t run without power; and a smart thermostat, security system, and Wi-Fi network they rely on every day,” he explains. “An outage is a lot different than it used to be—now it can mean you can’t work, can’t heat the house, and can’t charge your car.” Therefore, a standby generator has become a non-negotiable addition for many homeowners who can’t afford to have their power shut off for any period of time.

Standby generators are now recognized as being as necessary as smoke detectors and security systems, adding value to a home. According to Briggs & Stratton, a permanently installed generator could get you a 3 to 5 percent boost to your home value. And they are now more widespread and becoming the norm, so buyers expect to see them. “Most new builds automatically include a backup generator installation in the blueprints,” notes Woidan.

From a resale perspective, a home generator can help a property stand out by offering buyers peace of mind, especially in neighborhoods that have experienced repeated power disruptions, says Dell Jeanty, founder of Dell Residential Group in Arlington, Virginia. “A home with a generator during an outage demonstrates preparedness, which can be a meaningful selling point,” says Jeanty. “Some estimates suggest standby generators can recover as much as 95 percent of their installation cost at resale, although the actual return depends on the market, installation costs, and buyer demand.”

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Zach Lazzari, Additional research provided by Glenda Taylor, Timothy Dale

Published Nov 9, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

According to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), one foot of wet snow can weigh as much as 21 pounds per square foot—and that weight is exactly why using a roof rake can be essential to prevent damage.

To help you find the right tool for the job, we tested a range of different rakes on a tall shed and a camper after heavy snowfalls in Montana, working on metal and shingle roofs with different heights and pitches. Our favorite was the combo pack from Avalanche! since it can handle large amounts of snow and includes built-in wheels to prevent damage. Plus, it comes with different heads for different needs.

Keep reading to learn more about that model and the rest of the best roof rake options available.

Bottom line: Choosing the right roof rake can prevent damage and ensure safety during snow removal. Explore top picks and expert advice for the best options.

Note that roof rakes are intended for snow removal on single-story homes only. They should only be used when standing on the ground, and never while standing on a ladder. Attempting to balance a long pole while navigating snow-slick ladder rungs is a surefire way to slip and fall. Even if you have great balance, the weight of the snow you’re pulling off the roof could easily knock you off a ladder.

Selected for quality, functionality, material construction, and design, all of these tested products are excellent options for keeping the roof snow-free during the winter.

Equipped with a retractable plastic slide for enhanced efficiency, this rake pulls dislodged snow down the slide and off the roof, saving users time and effort. It’s also equipped with small wheels to help it glide along the roof without damaging it.

The rake extends from 4 to 15.5 feet when each fiberglass extension bar is attached. This process is simple, but it takes a few minutes to add each extension. With telescoping models being the exception, most other roof rakes use fitted extension segments similarly.

When adding an extension pole, users might need to remove gloves to press the locking button. I really liked the fiberglass poles because they aren’t nearly as cold as metal options. It is important to ensure that the segments are seated well at each joint, with the locking button in place.

Super durable, the plastic head is up to heavy-duty challenges. Raking snow off a roof is usually awkward with any rake, and that was the case with this one. But I didn’t mind a small amount of extra weight while reaching for the high spots because the durable design also gave me the confidence to hit the heavy snow spots and pull hard. I felt like the fiberglass poles were strong as well.

One other reason this won our top spot is the fact that multiple heads are included for different needs. The head that’s equipped with wheels and a slide should be able to tackle most users’ needs. The slide allows snow to fall off the roof easily, creating a pathway over gutters and other obstacles. When users hit stubborn areas and need a head that can bust through ice and grab big chunks of snow over shingles, asphalt, and tricky surfaces, they’ll want to use the rake head with wheels.

What our tester says: “I think this combo package is a great investment for anyone requiring regular use of a snow roof rake. Shoppers can find lighter-duty options for regions with less snow accumulation, but for those folks living in the mountains and regions where the snow piles up, I think this high-quality system is worth the price.”—Zach Lazzari, Product Tester and Writer

Read our full review: Avalanche! Combo Package

Get the Avalanche! Combo roof rake at The Home Depot.

The push-button telescoping design on this True Temper roof rake can extend the pole up to 17 feet, and it quickly collapses to 7 feet for storage. It weighs just 4.88 pounds, so users can easily lift it over their heads and control the movement of the rake.

If their home maintenance regularly requires removing substantial snow deposits, users will likely appreciate the lightweight aluminum design, which is easy to lift and maneuver thanks to its nonslip handle. Plus, this rake effectively pulls down deep snow accumulations in a single draw thanks to its 24-inch-wide poly blade.

This isn’t the longest roof rake out there, but its lightweight build is a trade-off that makes this model a favorite for large roofs. The telescoping handle lets the user quickly change the shaft’s length to match the required distance and pitch. Adjusting the telescoping handle is especially easy, and I found it very easy to manipulate. If you’ll be raking multiple roofs and will need to change lengths quickly, this is a great roof rake.

Although it’s a few feet shorter than some rakes, I was able to reach every spot needed on my roof. For a unique roof that requires some serious reach, there are much longer rakes out there, but they use segments rather than telescoping designs.

Get the True Temper roof rake at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Tractor Supply Co.

To properly clear a flat roof, it’s necessary to use a roof rake that doesn’t have a completely straight shaft. The shaft needs to be angled so that it can bend over the side and still sit flat on the roof. Designed with that in mind, this rake features a simple angled connector piece that fits onto the fiberglass shaft and extension bars. This gives users the ideal reach for a flat roof, like that of a truck trailer, RV, or shed.

Each extension bar is about 4 feet long, allowing the roof rake to extend to a maximum length of 15.5 feet. Also, keep in mind that each extension bar needs to be manually connected to the shaft. This is less convenient than other models that house the extensions inside the core of the shaft, allowing users to slide them out as desired. This roof rake weighs just over 7 pounds and features built-in wheels to keep the rake head from damaging the shingles.

I primarily tested this roof rake on my camper. It’s a flat roof with few obstacles aside from the two roof vents. The angled shaft made it very easy to clear the entire roof—it only took a few minutes. I think this model would also be great for semi-trailers, cargo trailers, and even flat roofs on garages and houses.

The problem with flat roofs is that they don’t allow snow to slough off naturally. This creates serious problem areas that can damage the roof and test the structural limits of a house or trailer. While straight-shaft models allow users to rake reasonably well, they still have trouble grabbing and pulling the base layers of snow. With this rake, I could easily clear the full snow load. It’s durable, sturdy, and easy to grip as well. I’m a big fan of this model and the quality of this brand’s products in general.

Get the Avalanche! Big Rig roof rake at Amazon.

Dealing with stand-alone pole extension segments can be a hassle at times. Not only is it a pain to have to lug them around while raking the roof, but it also takes time and planning to add and remove segments for different areas of the roof. It’s true that segmented designs work well for users who have a specific length need and consistent roof pitches—it’s not a bad system by any means, but all-in-one telescoping handles are much more convenient.

When you need to make adjustments on the fly and don’t want a pile of poles in the garage or truck, a telescoping handle design is an ideal option. This telescoping roof rake from Garant features a well-rounded design with a smooth-telescoping handle that extends to 16.5 feet long. It’s certainly not the longest out there, but it should be sufficient for most single-story homes.

I loved the handle and pole design of this model. It slides out in seconds, so length can be added or subtracted in a jiffy. I found the push-button design very user-friendly. Just make sure to hear a click to lock out the handle at the desired length. The coated primary pole also offers a great gripping platform for the second hand.

This model uses a standard poly blade with angled supports. The same system can be found on many other models. It’s sturdy and makes it easy to grab and pull snow. It requires more effort and strength than roller-and-slide systems, but I still found it easy to get the job done. For anyone with a normal single-story home, this roof rake is a winner. I love that it’s easy to store as a single-piece unit rather than having to deal with various poles and components.

Get the Garant roof rake at Ace Hardware.

Testing was done throughout a weeklong storm event. The first 3 days received heavy snowfall with a mix of dry powder and wet snow. The powder wasn’t problematic, but the wet snow was heavy, and it stuck to the rooftops. It also underwent a slight thaw and a subsequent freeze cycle that solidified the rooftop snow.

I waited for the storm to end and rotated through each roof rake, pulling sections of snow down. I judged each roof rake based on ease of assembly, grip, length, and ability to reach and grab snow without damaging the roof. Durability was also considered. Several of the brands have similar design features with slight variations in the way they are constructed. There was a reasonable overlap when it comes to performance and function with these look-alike models.

Make sure you’re up to date on the most important product factors before deciding on the best option to rake snow from your roof and prevent ice dams from forming. Some factors to consider in finding the right snow rake for roof cleaning include the type and quality of the materials, length, weight, and head design.

A roof rake for snow removal can be made of different materials, including fiberglass, polyethylene, aluminum, and wood.

Most roof rakes come with adjustable poles that can be lengthened from 14 to 22 feet for snow removal and shortened to less than 8 feet for storage. The longer the pole, the higher users will be able to reach on the roof, but longer poles can also be unwieldy and may require more physical strength to lift and maneuver.

Roof rakes range in weight between 4 and 14 pounds, with most of the weight in the rake head. The heavier the rake head, the more likely it is to sink deeply into the snow on the roof, allowing users to remove a good amount with each pull. Conversely, heavy roof rakes require more physical strength to lift and position.

Roof rake heads range in depth from a narrow 3 inches to a generous 10 inches, and widths run between 12 and 24 inches. The larger the rake head, the more snow the rake can remove in a single pull. If the snow is wet and heavy, it can require additional physical strength to pull it, which can lead to back and shoulder fatigue.

Curved heads and interchangeable attachments, such as a scoop, blade, or plastic slide, can greatly decrease fatigue if used properly. It’s also a good idea to consider looking for a roof rake with built-in wheels or bumpers to help protect the roof and shingles from damage. This is especially important when working with an aluminum rake head or if the rake has a blade attachment.

When starting to rake the snow off of a roof, it’s important to begin the process by removing the snow from the roof’s edge first. If users attempt to extend the roof rake as much as possible and simply pull down any snow caught within this range, there is a good chance that they will be unable to move the snow. Also, keep in mind that even if the snow does move, it isn’t a good idea to bring down that much snow at once because the weight of the snow could cause injury.

While the goal of snow removal on a driveway is to clear any snow or ice that could cause the car to slip, it’s not actually necessary to rake every inch of snow off the roof. Leaving one or two inches of snow isn’t going to cause ice dams to form, and this gap can help prevent the roof shingles from being damaged during raking.

Additionally, under no circumstances should users attempt to climb a ladder or walk on a sloped roof in winter conditions to remove snow. The entire purpose of a roof rake is for the user to remain on the ground, so don’t risk trying to rake the roof while perched on a ladder.

For more information on the best roof rake for snow removal at your home, take a look at some of the most commonly asked questions and the detailed answers below.

Unlike general-purpose rakes, snow rakes (also known as roof rakes) are specially designed for one purpose: to remove snow from single-story roofs without having to climb. This makes it much easier and safer to keep the roof clear of snow and prevent ice dams from forming in the gutter system.

The blade on a roof rake head can damage the shingles on a roof. This is especially true with aluminum rake heads, but this problem can be avoided if you invest in a roof rake with built-in wheels. These wheels elevate the rake slightly, suspending the rake head above the surface of the shingles instead of grating against them.

If you rake the roof the same day it snows, you can prevent ice build-up in the gutter system.

Whether or not you need a roof rake depends on how much snow naturally builds up on your roof. Some houses have steep roofs that don’t collect a lot of snow, while others may have a gentle slope. Metal roofs can be raked with a roof rake to keep them clear of snow, but in most cases, the snow will tend to slide off a metal roof without a problem. In fact, many homes with metal roofs need snow guards or snow fences to prevent piles of snow from sliding off and potentially hurting anyone standing nearby.

It’s a good idea to rake the roof on the same day it snows, just as it isn’t wise to wait long to shovel your driveway. Keep in mind that freshly fallen snow is much easier to move than snow that has been allowed to melt and refreeze under the sun.

#7724. Your Level Might Be the Wrong Size, and It Could Be Throwing Off Your Work

A short level works for some projects, but longer surfaces need a wider check. Learn how to pick the right size and use it accurately.

Levels come in many different shapes and sizes, and figuring out how long a level should be for a certain project isn’t always straightforward. Choosing the right size matters because a level that’s too short can miss uneven spots, while one that’s too long can be difficult to use in tight spaces.

Here’s how much of a surface a level should cover, which sizes work best, and when overhang is okay.

It depends on the project, but a longer level is usually better for checking bigger surfaces. A shorter one might show that the middle of a board is level without catching a problem closer to either end.

The level doesn’t have to stretch across the entire surface, though. A 24-inch level can work on a four-foot shelf, for example, as long as the installer checks several spots along its length. For longer surfaces, a smaller level can sit on a long, straight board to check a wider area. A laser level is another option, especially when lining up things across a room.

The way the level sits on the material matters, too. A little sawdust or dirt underneath can affect the reading, so both surfaces should be clean. The tool also needs to sit firmly without rocking.

There’s no set rule for how much of a surface a level needs to cover, but it should fit comfortably and have enough contact to stay steady.

Different sizes work better for different jobs:

“Use a 4-foot carpenter’s level for framing whenever you have room for its length,” according to The Home Depot. “Warps or waves in the boards can throw off a shorter carpenter’s level.”

Another common concern is whether the level can hang over the edge of whatever is being checked. Some overhang is fine, provided the tool has enough support to stay steady.

If it starts tipping or rocking, a shorter level will likely work better. The bubble doesn’t need to be directly above the material, either. It can still give an accurate reading even when that part of the tool hangs past the edge.

#7723. New York State Bar Association tells lawyers not to bill for time saved by AI

The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use them. (Image from Shutterstock)

The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use them.

Law360 reported Monday that the state bar association’s Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies issued a report classifying the cost of buying and maintaining such software as an overhead expense that can be passed along as a disbursement only when tied to a specific client matter and when the basis for the charge has been disclosed.

According to Law360, the report added that lawyers generally don’t have to tell clients about AI use for administrative tasks—such as word processing, spelling and grammar checks, calendaring or timekeeping—provided that the use doesn’t affect fees.

“Generative AI is indelibly changing the practice of law. As part of our mission to be the leading voice for the legal profession, we are providing clear guidelines on the use of AI tools as a resource, so attorneys can use AI responsibly and ethically in their practices,” said Taa Grays, the president of the New York State Bar Association, in a statement. “The guidelines can help attorneys avoid possible perils of using AI, including inadvertently practicing law in a jurisdiction where they are not licensed or failing to notify clients or the courts of AI use.”

The committee also flagged familiar hazards, such as biased training data that may deepen existing inequities. Confidentiality is another concern: If an AI tool learns from one client’s information in a way that makes it available in another client’s matter, lawyers must turn to the New York Rules of Professional Conduct.

The report cautioned against building tools that deliver automated legal services in ways that could amount to unauthorized practice or using AI to pass as a human with prospective clients.

Supervising lawyers were reminded that they remain responsible for their subordinates’ compliance and should not assume that a law firm-approved tool or policy removes the need to review work on each matter.

According to Law360, the state bar association’s governing body adopted the report Saturday.

The fate of billable hours is in the hands of artificial intelligence
