#7708. A World of Independent Nations

Introduction

It is a great pleasure to be here in Jerusalem, and it is especially fitting to discuss “A World of Independent Nations” here in Israel. If any nation understands the importance of sovereignty, national survival, secure borders, and the sometimes inconvenient necessity of putting its own people first, it is Israel.

I come here as an American conservative, as someone who has spent much of his career working on Europe, and I should probably confess at the outset, as an unreconstructed Euroskeptic. I realize that admitting you are a Euroskeptic at NatCon is not exactly an act of great personal courage. It is rather like announcing at Heritage that you have reservations about socialism or Islamism.

But I want to make a broader argument today.

National sovereignty and transatlantic cooperation are not opposites. They are not even in tension. Properly understood, national sovereignty is the basis for meaningful transatlantic cooperation.

For far too long, the foreign policy establishment on both sides of the Atlantic has presented us with a false choice. Either you believe in an ever more integrated West, governed by international institutions and supranational bureaucracies, or you retreat into isolationism. Either Brussels runs Europe, or Europe falls apart. Either Washington manages its allies, or America abandons them.

I reject that choice. There is another model. It is a world of sovereign nations that know who they are, control their own borders, govern themselves, defend themselves, and cooperate when their interests and values coincide—in other words, exactly the sort of international order conservatives should be trying to build.

The Nation-State Is Not the Problem

For the past several decades, nationalism has been treated in much of polite Western society almost as a pathology. Europe in particular was told that its terrible 20th-century history proved that the nation-state itself had failed.

The answer was integration. Then, more integration. Then, when integration produced problems, the answer was invariably still more integration. It reminds me a little of the old joke about socialism: The reason it has never worked is apparently because nobody has ever tried quite enough of it.

The European project originally presented itself as cooperation among sovereign countries. But over time, political authority moved steadily away from national governments and toward institutions increasingly removed from national electorates. As I argued in “U.S. First Principles vs. European Bureaucratic Overreach,” the European Union has increasingly transferred authority away from sovereign nations and into distant institutions with limited democratic accountability.[REF]

This matters because democracy requires a Demos. Someone has to be able to answer the simplest political question there is: Who governs? And if you dislike the answer: How do you get rid of them?

That is easy to understand in a nation-state. It becomes considerably less clear when authority is dispersed among commissioners, courts, councils, agencies, treaties, and qualified-majority voting. It is difficult enough getting rid of a bad congressman. Try voting out the European Commission.

Europe Is Not the European Union

This leads to a distinction that American policymakers repeatedly fail to make: Europe is not the European Union. Europe is a civilization. Europe is a collection of ancient nations. Europe is Britain and France, Poland and Hungary, Italy and Greece, the Baltic States and the Nordic countries, and many others, each with its own history, traditions, loyalties, interests, and democratic institutions. The European Union is an institution.

The two are not synonymous. In fact, one of the most damaging habits in American foreign policy has been to confuse support for Europe with support for European integration. An America First foreign policy should stop doing that.

As I argued recently after Iceland rejected renewed EU accession talks in “Iceland Puts the Freeze on Brussels’ ‘Ever Closer Union,’” Washington should deal with Europe as it actually exists: as a continent of nations. America benefits when democratic allies control their own resources and interests and cooperate voluntarily, including through NATO.[REF]

That is not anti-European. It is profoundly pro-European. It says that the Czech Republic belongs to the Czechs. Poland belongs to the Poles. Hungary belongs to the Hungarians. Britain belongs to the British. And the United States belongs to Americans.

Perhaps this is considered radical these days. I prefer to call it self-government.

America First Does Not Mean America Alone

This brings me to America First.

America First is sometimes caricatured, particularly in Europe, as a doctrine of withdrawal. I think that completely misunderstands it. America First does not mean America alone. It means that American foreign policy should advance American interests.

And we should expect our friends to do exactly the same thing for their countries. America does not want European governments that obediently ask Washington what to do. America wants strong allies. America wants European countries capable of securing their borders, growing their economies, and defending their territory. America wants European NATO members capable of bearing a much larger share of the burden of defending Europe. America wants allies, not dependencies.

That is why sovereignty actually strengthens transatlanticism. America does not ultimately form alliances with regulatory systems. It forms alliances with nations capable of making decisions and honoring commitments.

A weak country that has surrendered responsibility for vital decisions is not made stronger merely because it sits inside a larger bureaucracy. A self-confident nation that can defend itself, control its territory, and act politically is a much more useful ally.

Where Conservatives Must Cooperate

But this cannot mean conservatives retreating behind their own borders and ignoring one another. Quite the opposite: Each nation must decide questions of free speech, border control, family, faith, energy, economic freedom, and defense for itself—but those debates increasingly reach across the Atlantic.

We should be candid. President Trump’s style can sometimes unsettle even our European conservative friends who agree with him on borders, sovereignty, and burden-sharing. That is no reason to abandon cooperation. European conservatives need not become Trumpists. Friends can disagree over tactics, trade, Ukraine, or NATO and still work together where their interests and principles coincide.

So, what should cooperation look like? It should begin with permanent working relationships among think tanks, lawmakers, legal groups, and campaigners. It should be built around particular battles, not a single manifesto. We can cooperate on free speech without agreeing on every foreign policy question.

And it should connect sovereign actors directly: Congress with national parliaments, attorneys general with legal advocates, and governments with governments—not everything mediated through Brussels.

The agenda is clear: speech, borders, family, faith, energy, economic freedom, and defense.

The test is simple. Cooperation should make each nation more capable of governing itself, not less.

A Practical Framework: A Transatlantic Conservative Compact

I propose a Transatlantic Conservative Compact. Not a treaty. Not a bureaucracy. And certainly not a conservative Brussels.

It would be a voluntary network linking conservative governments, lawmakers, think tanks, and legal groups around specific projects. Small working groups could share model laws, legal briefs, and campaign lessons on speech, borders, family, energy, and defense. Members could join one project and decline another.

That is the model. Not uniformity: cooperation.

Free speech is the obvious place to begin because rules written in Brussels or London can govern American platforms and affect what American users see.

The EU’s Digital Services Act can fine the largest platforms according to global turnover.[REF] In 2024, EU Commissioner Thierry Breton even warned Elon Musk before his interview with Donald Trump—an American political event.[REF] Britain’s Online Safety Act can likewise reach services based abroad and impose enormous fines.[REF] Faced with that risk, platforms will often censor first and ask questions later.

American and European conservatives should expose these demands, challenge them in court, and defend clear legal protections for political and religious speech. Alliance Defending Freedom, among others, is doing stellar work in this area.

In “European Democracy Shield: A Threat to Free Speech and Democratic Accountability,” I argued that American and European conservatives need to work more closely together to protect freedom of speech and conscience.[REF]

Border control and mass migration are another such issue. Individual nations must decide whom they admit, who is entitled to remain, and what obligations newcomers owe to the society receiving them. That responsibility cannot simply be outsourced upward.

Borders are not an embarrassing leftover from an unenlightened past. They mark the territory within which democratic government operates. If a government cannot determine who enters its country or effectively enforce its immigration law, we should ask in what meaningful sense it remains sovereign.

Here, American and European conservatives have a great deal to learn from each other. The objective should not be identical policies imposed from above. It should be the exchange of ideas among sovereign governments pursuing the interests of their own citizens.

That also means confronting Islamification directly. Religious liberty must be protected, but political Islam and parallel societies must not be tolerated. Newcomers who wish to live in Western nations must accept our laws, our civic order, and our civilizational inheritance. They need to integrate—or leave.

A Transatlantic Conservative Compact would also involve working together on issues like energy security, economic freedom, family policy, religious liberty, and the defense of Western civilization—and, of course, defense.

The transatlantic alliance remains important, but NATO should be an alliance of sovereign countries accepting reciprocal obligations, not a mechanism for permanently transferring responsibility for European security to the American taxpayer. If European nations are sovereign, then sovereignty comes with responsibilities. One of them is paying for your own defense.

I suspect even my European friends will concede that this particular American enthusiasm for national sovereignty is unlikely to disappear.

Europe Beyond the EU

At Heritage’s Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom, this is increasingly becoming a central part of our work.

Heritage is organizing a major event in Washington called “Europe Beyond the EU.” Its starting point is deliberately provocative: What if the future of Europe is not deeper integration? What if the real intellectual challenge is to imagine European cooperation after the age of centralization? In this tenth-anniversary year of the Brexit referendum, our December 8, 2026, conference will open that conversation, exploring what a European order rooted in sovereign nation-states might look like and how American conservatives can support it.

And we intend to go much further. Our planned Transatlantic Sovereignty Initiative will develop practical alternatives to centralized control over democracy, speech, trade, energy, economic policy, borders, and security. The purpose is not simply to criticize Brussels. It is to develop a positive conservative architecture for cooperation among self-governing nations.

That distinction matters. Euroskepticism cannot simply mean saying “No.” Eventually, we have to explain what we are saying “Yes” to. The answer is a flexible Europe.

  • NATO for collective defense.
  • Bilateral and multilateral agreements where they make sense.
  • Trade among free nations.
  • Voluntary arrangements on security and migration.
  • Cooperation without political absorption.
  • Partnership without permanent centralization.

I have called this elsewhere a functional Europe: sovereign nations using the institution appropriate to the task rather than assuming every problem requires transferring yet another power upward.[REF] That principle works beyond Europe as well.

Conservative Solidarity Without Conservative Globalism

There is, however, a trap here for our own movement. Conservatives rightly criticize globalism. We should therefore be rather careful not to invent a conservative globalism of our own. Our purpose cannot be to replace one transnational ideological establishment with another.

A Hungarian conservative will naturally put Hungary first. A Polish conservative should put Poland first. An Israeli conservative should—and most definitely does—put Israel first. And I make no apology for saying that an American conservative should put America first.

The miracle is not that our interests will always be identical. They won’t. The opportunity is that sovereign nations which possess civilizational confidence can nevertheless recognize enormous areas of common interest.

We can defend the freedom to speak.

We can defend religious liberty.

We can defend the family.

We can secure our borders.

We can resist unelected bureaucracies claiming powers voters never willingly surrendered.

We can defend the inheritance of Western civilization without demanding that every Western nation become politically identical.

And we can maintain a strong Atlantic alliance without asking either Americans or Europeans to surrender their independence.

That is my idea of transatlantic conservative solidarity. Not bland uniformity: solidarity. Not supranational government: cooperation. Not a homogenized West administered from Washington, Brussels, Davos, or anywhere else: a West of free nations.

Conclusion

For most of my professional life, the dominant assumption has been that history was moving relentlessly away from the nation-state. National loyalties were supposedly becoming obsolete. Borders would matter less. Supranational institutions would inevitably become stronger. Politics would become increasingly managerial. And ordinary voters would eventually learn to accept all of this.

I am increasingly convinced that precisely the opposite is happening. The nation has returned because it never really went away.

People want government close enough to control. They want borders that mean something. They want political leaders who are accountable to them. They want to preserve what makes their country their country. And they are increasingly impatient with institutions that tell them these desires are somehow illegitimate.

This is not a crisis for democracy. It is democracy reasserting itself. The challenge for conservatives is to turn that democratic revolt into a durable political order.

A world of independent nations need not be a world of isolation. It can be a world of vigorous cooperation precisely because that cooperation is voluntary.

A confident America should want confident allies. A sovereign Europe can be a better American partner than an increasingly centralized European Union. And nations secure in their own identity are better able to cooperate because they do not fear that cooperation requires their disappearance.

So my argument today is ultimately very simple: Sovereignty is not the enemy of Western unity. It is the foundation of it.

The future of transatlanticism should not be ever closer union. It should be ever stronger nations: independent, democratic, self-confident, able to disagree, able to cooperate, able to defend themselves, and willing, when our principles and interests align, to stand together.

That is the transatlantic alliance worth defending, and that is a world of independent nations worth building.

Paul McCarthy is Senior Research Fellow for European Affairs in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation. This lecture is adapted from remarks delivered at NatCon Jerusalem on October 8, 2026.

#7707. Poe, the Pandemic and a Halloween Lesson for Catholics and Protestants

For many years, I kept a private rule as some men keep a flask in their coat pocket: one novel always at hand, open somewhere, patient, no matter how the briefs and research and obligations piled up.

Lately, I have broken the rule. I’ve felt its absence the way the tongue keeps returning to the place where a tooth once was. Then, the other afternoon, a television appearance was abruptly canceled, and I found myself holding two unclaimed hours like dollar bills found on the sidewalk. The day was bright and sunny, but it was October all the same. The light had that thin, cidery quality, and the shadows lay longer on the lawn than the clock said they had any right to.

It is, as friends of mine insist, Kirktober. Russell Kirk, the sage of Mecosta, Mich., whose “The Conservative Mind” gave postwar conservatism both its pedigree and its conscience, was born in October, and he loved nothing better than a ghost story told by firelight at Piety Hill, his ancestral house. He wrote them too, and wrote them well, for he believed the uncanny was a moral instrument: it reminds us that the universe keeps rules we did not write.

So, in his honor, I wandered from my usual shelves, took down an old leatherbound Poe whose spine had gone soft as a glove, and let it fall open where it wished. It chose “The Masque of the Red Death.”

>>> Manhattan’s Lost Its Screen Presence

The story is hardly longer than a sermon, and it haunted me in a way Poe could not have intended, because the plague years (yes, I mean COVID are not far behind us. His pestilence is “fatal” and “hideous.” “Blood was its Avatar and its seal—the redness and the horror of blood.” The whole business, from first dizziness to last breath, took half an hour.

And then there is Prince Prospero, whose very name is a boast of good fortune and an echo of Shakespeare’s magician, the one who withdrew to an island and commanded the weather. Poe’s prince gathers a thousand of his gayest knights and dames and retires “to the deep seclusion of one of his castellated abbeys.” The courtiers weld the bolts shut behind them. The external world could take care of itself.

One remembers the photographs from our own season of quarantine: the governors at the fine restaurants, the masks lowered for the cameras of the important, the rules that fell on ordinary people like rain and somehow never dampened those who made them.

Inside the abbey, Poe builds a fever dream. There are seven rooms, each a single color: blue, purple, green, orange, white, violet. The seventh is hung in black velvet, and its windows are scarlet, the deep color of blood. No lamp burns in any chamber; instead, braziers on tripods stand outside the tinted glass, throwing firelight through the panes so that every room swims in its own unnatural hue.

Here the masquerade whirls on. The costumes have much of the beautiful, much of the wanton, much of the bizarre, something of the terrible. A mask is a small lie that promises a large one: that you may become anyone, and so nothing can find you. But in the black room stands a great ebony clock, and on each hour it sounds a note so strange that the orchestra falters, the waltzers freeze, the giddiest go pale. The clock is the one guest who cannot be bribed. The rooms run east to west, dawn to dusk, and everyone knows where the last one leads.

At midnight, an intruder appears: 

The figure was tall and gaunt, and shrouded from head to foot in the habiliments of the grave. The mask which concealed the visage was made so nearly to resemble the countenance of a stiffened corpse that the closest scrutiny must have had difficulty in detecting the cheat. 

Prospero, furious at the insult, chases the figure through all seven rooms with a drawn dagger. In the black chamber, the stranger turns, the dagger drops, and the prince falls dead upon the sable carpet. The revelers seize the masker and find beneath the shroud and the corpse-like mask nothing at all, the garments “untenanted by any tangible form.” The Red Death has come and gone.

Poe knew this guest personally. Tuberculosis took his young mother when he was two, then his foster mother, then his brother. In January 1842, a few months before this story appeared, his wife, Virginia, was singing at the piano when blood came into her mouth. She lingered five years. The Red Death lived among him and his and was not merely the product of fiction.

>>> The Hidden Jewel at Jacksonville State

My mother would have shut the book. She hated stories like these and would not let us celebrate what she considered the devil’s holiday, so my brother and I were costumed in innocence: pirates, Batman and Robin, Superman, a clown, a nerd with tape on his spectacles, Auburn football players in orange and blue.

We could trick-or-treat, but as we grew older, we went instead to youth group for the Reformation Celebration, honoring Luther and his hammer on that same last night of October. Only as a grown man did I understand how my Catholic brethren must see such a party: as a festival of the Church’s broken body, a wound that Protestants and Catholics alike ought to mourn.

Kirk himself crossed that divide, entering the Catholic Church in middle age, and I think he would have seen what Poe’s story finally tells us. Prospero believed walls could save him. Not so long ago, all of us believed it, or were told to. We sealed ourselves in our own abbeys, masked our faces, and watched the clock of the daily COVID death count, while the powerful went on dancing in rooms we were not permitted to enter.

The churches went dark that spring, Catholic and Protestant both, and the old quarrel between them seemed suddenly beside the point. The Mass and the Lord’s Supper were suspended alike; the dying went to God alone, with no priest or pastor at the bedside; and Easter came to empty pews on both sides of the Reformation.

For a season, the divided church was united in the one way none of us would have chosen: in absence. Perhaps that was the lesson. Nothing we bolt shut keeps out the stranger at midnight, and the clock strikes for every room. What the dark cannot touch is what we share. All Hallows’ Eve is only the night before All Saints, and the night of masks gives way, at last, to the morning of faces.

#7706. Justice Department Announces Coordinated Actions to Combat North Korean Remote IT Worker Schemes Affecting More Than 70 U.S. Companies

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through remote information technology (IT) work for U.S. companies. These actions include an indictment, two arrests, searches of multiple known or suspected “laptop farms” in Texas pursuant to “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” and the seizure of approximately 187 computer devices used by DPRK IT workers.

“North Korea’s rogue regime uses its pervasive IT worker schemes to raise revenue for various illicit purposes, including the development of weapons that could ultimately target the United States or its allies,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “These schemes threaten the security of the IT systems and data of the deceived U.S. employers and leave countless victims of identity theft. NSD, along with our law enforcement partners, will use every available tool to track down anyone assisting the DPRK and to protect our national security.”

“Threats posed by nation-states like North Korea are a stark reminder that our adversaries will go to great measures to exploit our nation’s economic strength to further and fuel their own nefarious agendas,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “We are thankful to FBI Cleveland for their incredible work and persistence to put a stop to these bad actors. These charges serve as an urgent alert to all U.S. companies to remain vigilant in their hiring practices.”

“This investigation is about far more than fraud,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas. “It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders. Every laptop farm we dismantle shuts down a revenue stream that the North Korean government relies on to fund weapons programs that threaten global stability. Operation Lonestar Roundup sends a clear message: we will not allow enemies of the United States to exploit our businesses or compromise our national security.”

“North Korea continues to deploy remote IT workers using stolen identities to infiltrate American companies and generate revenue for the regime and its weapons programs,” said Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Division. “Today, the FBI and DOJ announced a series of coordinated actions against this threat, securing charges against 14 individuals, conducting two arrests, seizing nearly 190 devices, and executing operations at more than 40 suspected ‘laptop farms’ across Texas. Close coordination between the private sector and federal law enforcement was central to this operation. To further combat the threat, the FBI has issued a Public Service Announcement with detailed mitigation guidance for U.S. companies.”

Sun Sheng Ming, et al. Indictment and Arrests – Northern District of Ohio

Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio announced the arrests of U.S. nationals Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas pursuant to a four-count wire fraud, money laundering, and identity theft indictment. The indictment describes a multi-year fraud scheme by Bostelle, Pena, and their co-conspirators to obtain remote IT work with U.S. companies that generated more than $3 million in revenue. The indictment also charges China-based Sun Sheng Ming, Pei Li Guang, Weng Shou Cheng, Han Guo Bin, Wang Jian Jun, Sheng Zhang Kun, Zhang Wei Ping, Zhang Li Ping, Yu Yang, Jin Long for their roles in the scheme. The identities of two additional defendants remain under seal.

According to the indictment, from 2019 to in or around July 2025, DPRK IT workers applied for and obtained remote positions by using stolen or fabricated identity documents, virtual private networks and proxy infrastructure to appear as though they were U.S. persons working from within the United States. They also relied on U.S.-based facilitators who received and hosted multiple laptop computers — issued by victim U.S. companies — at their residences in the United States (“laptop farms”), housed and configured those devices, installed remote-access software and transferred earnings to DPRK‑controlled accounts.

In total, the scheme impacted more than 70 U.S. company employers and generated approximately $3 million in revenue for IT workers. The revenue is believed to have been sent to sanctioned entities controlled by the DPRK. Victim employers included companies in the health care, communications, cyber support, retail, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio, sixteen additional states, and the District of Columbia.

The FBI Cleveland Field Office is investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Duncan T. Brown for the Northern District of Ohio and Trial Attorney Neeraj Gupta of the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section are prosecuting the case.

Operation Lonestar Roundup Disrupts Multiple Known or Suspected Laptop Farms in Texas

Between Sept. 21 and Sept. 25, the FBI conducted searches and other law enforcement action at over 40 residences in Texas known to be, or suspected of operating as, laptop farms for DPRK IT workers. Over the course of the entire operation (Operation Lonestar Roundup), the FBI seized approximately 187 laptops and KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) devices that DPRK IT workers and their U.S.-based facilitators used to commit fraud, obtain remote employment, and generate revenue for the North Korean regime’s sanctioned weapons programs. U.S. cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has identified this group of DPRK IT workers and their helpers as “Famous Chollima.”

Investigators discovered that the DPRK operatives allegedly used a network of fraudulent email accounts to facilitate their criminal activity. The following accounts were among those identified as being used in these schemes:

Employers are encouraged to add these accounts to the list of indicators they use to identify and disrupt DPRK IT worker employment.

Today, the FBI published a public service announcement describing the evolving DPRK IT worker threat, including tips on how to detect the threat. Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals. Additionally, CrowdStrike today published a blog post describing its efforts at monitoring customer networks for DPRK IT worker activity and its successful collaboration with the FBI to disrupt this threat.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas, the FBI’s Dallas Field Office, and the FBI’s Cyber Division coordinated Operation Lonestar Roundup. Valuable assistance was provided by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio.

Today’s announcements represent the Department’s latest actions to combat North Korean IT worker schemes as part of a joint NSD and FBI Cyber and Counterintelligence Divisions effort, the DPRK RevGen: Domestic Enabler Initiative. This effort prioritizes targeting and disrupting the DPRK’s illicit revenue generation schemes and its U.S.-based enablers. The Department previously announced other actions pursuant to the initiative, including in June 2025, November 2025, April 2026, and May 2026.

As described in Public Service Announcements published in May 2024, January 2025, July 2025, and today, North Korean remote IT workers posing as legitimate remote IT workers have committed data extortion and exfiltrated the proprietary and sensitive data from U.S. companies. DPRK IT worker schemes typically involve the use of stolen identities, alias emails, social media, online cross-border payment platforms, and online job site accounts, as well as false websites, proxy computers, and witting and unwitting third parties located in the U.S. and elsewhere. North Korean IT workers leverage these third parties, which include U.S.-based individuals, to gain fraudulent employment and access to U.S. company networks to generate this revenue.

Other public advisories about the threats, red flag indicators, and potential mitigation measures for these schemes include a May 2022 advisory released by the FBI, Department of the Treasury, and Department of State; a July 2023 advisory from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence; and guidance issued in October 2023 by the United States and the Republic of Korea (South Korea). As described the May 2022 advisory, North Korean IT workers have been known individually to earn up to $300,000 annually, generating hundreds of millions of dollars collectively each year, on behalf of designated entities, such as the North Korean Ministry of Defense and others directly involved in the DPRK’s weapons programs.

The U.S. Department of State has offered potential rewards for up to $5 million in support of international efforts to disrupt the DPRK’s illicit financial activities, including for cybercrimes, money laundering, and sanctions evasion.

The details in the above-described court documents are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7704. Setting Guidelines for Using AI in the Classroom

Teachers are doing their best to guide student use of artificial intelligence, but it’s clear that some boundaries are desperately needed.

Stop signs are common. Before the start of this school year, New York City officials banned the use of generative AI for public preschools through eighth grade, and Los Angeles educators banned access to generative AI platforms on school devices for all grade levels.

Parents seem to agree: In recent polls, 75% of them reported supporting pausing AI in schools. But a nearly identical share of respondents (73%) say children already use AI for schoolwork. The technology is here, and let’s face it: Pauses aren’t a long-term solution. Teachers and children need clear guidelines.

AI, after all, is embedded in many online platforms. Alphabet (Google’s parent company) has offered discounted Chromebooks to schools since at least 2011, and Gemini is included in Google’s Chrome web browser. Since Google does not allow its AI summaries or chatbot to be turned off, Fairfax County Public Schools developed its own plug-in to block Google AI search results.

>>> Families and Students Need Guidance on AI

School districts across the country are deciding which forms of AI to ban and for which grade levels, but those choosing to use AI would do well to consider proactive uses of the technology and methods for responsible integration.

State lawmakers must define academic standards and adopt appropriate guardrails for responsible use of AI in classrooms. At its worst, students use AI for companionship in place of friends and to do their homework or write their essays. At its best, students use AI to find, collect, and distill information and identify errors in their own work. AI learning platforms can measure student proficiency in a lesson and build exercises according to their level, following teacher-led instruction.

Even New York City’s restrictions are not banning all forms of AI at the lower grades. City officials allow for the use of programs such as Quill, which helps students with reading comprehension and research and Edia, a math program.

The Heritage Foundation developed model legislation for AI in schools that allows for responsible use of AI in classrooms. The model prioritizes human-centered learning and oversight, transparency, safety and data security. Schools should not be required to adopt AI into lesson plans, but for those that do, educators should help students recognize the difference between getting assistance with homework questions and plagiarism.

State lawmakers should respect parent rights and require schools to obtain parent consent for AI use. Educators should offer parents and students alternatives when families choose to opt out. AI vendors should not gather student data for targeted advertising or sell or rent this information.

Likewise, educators must adhere to state and federal privacy laws such as the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act.

While school officials can allow generative AI programs, teachers should prohibit the use of AI companions that mimic personal relationships. Romantic conversations or simulated friendships do not have academic use and interfere with children’s social skills and healthy development.

>>> The Promise and Peril of Artificial Intelligence in Education  

Florida recently adopted rules for AI in schools that are consistent with many of these provisions. State officials recognize that teachers and students can use AI effectively and banning AI will not eliminate the use of large language models (LLMs) but cause the activity to go unmonitored. If AI use goes underground, the potential for cheating increases, with potentially disastrous consequences for student learning.

Lawmakers should use lessons already available in research and in the media on effective and ineffective uses of technology to advance policy ideas dedicated to protecting student privacy and promoting student learning. Educators can harness the benefits that come from new technologies like AI to help students extend their abilities and not erase them.

State officials should adopt thoughtfully designed boundaries for student and teacher use of AI, including restrictions on non-academic uses of AI. These provisions can allow teachers to blend AI into instructional guidance and help prepare students for the future. AI is part of that future, so let’s use it to our advantage.

#7703. No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability

Of the many inane comments that socialists have made this year, the one that democracy is “the building block of socialism” might be the most absurd.

Who made the comment? You guessed it: New York City’s boy genius, Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

In a recent episode of “This Past Weekend,” Mr. Mamdani discussed socialism’s ability to ensure affordability with comedian Theo Von. The interview was replete with Marxian nonsense, but Mr. Mamdani also discussed many Americans’ economic frustrations: homeownership feels out of reach; rent is expensive; childcare is unaffordable; and grocery prices are substantially higher.

Young people increasingly feel that the American dream is “slipping away.”

Recognizing affordability problems, however, is not the same as identifying the causes. Mr. Mamdani avers that the free market system cannot solve these problems and that socialism is the silver bullet.

Consider his assertion about democracy. When Mr. Von brought up the concept, Mr. Mamdani interrupted him and claimed, “That’s the building block of socialism.”

>>> Mamdani’s City Grocery Plan Could Leave Taxpayers Paying for Every Banana

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels would like to have a word.

To them, it was clear that implementing socialism—a word that they used interchangeably with communism—would require the opposite of democracy: tyranny.

In their 1848 “The Communist Manifesto,” the owner’s manual for Marxism, Marx and Engels rightly predicted that people would fight back when the government seized their property—something Mr. Mamdani should bear in mind as he upsets more and more New Yorkers with property-grabbing schemes.

“The proletariat will use its political supremacy to wrest, by degrees, all capital from the bourgeoisie, to centralize all instruments of production in the hands of the State,” Marx and Engels wrote. “Of course, in the beginning, this cannot be effected except by means of despotic inroads on the rights of property, and on the conditions of bourgeois production.”

So, no, Mr. Mamdani. Socialism’s pillars are totalitarian, based on forced nationalization and coercive state control.

Now, let us deal with the fanciful claim that socialism is the best way to order society: “Socialism to me means that you have whatever you need to live a dignified life, and it’s the government’s job to deliver on that.”

It sounds compassionate, but what happens when the government assumes responsibility for determining, financing and delivering the necessities of a “dignified life”?

Here, we begin to understand why Mr. Mamdani mixes socialism with democracy. To him, democracy is not just about electing leaders; it is also about letting people choose things that they cannot afford, courtesy of taxpayers.

In line with his big-government agenda, he explained socialism as “the extension of democracy from the ballot box to the rest of your life … your workplace, your home.”

Yet socialists devalue real democracy when they define it as the “right” for people to own what they have not earned. They also devalue the protection of inalienable rights when they insist that 51% of the electorate can suppress individual liberties such as property rights—something America’s Founders called “mobocracy.”

A free society empowers majorities, but it also protects individual rights. More government intervention will neither expand liberty nor make New York City more affordable.

The Big Apple is indeed the most expensive city in the United States and the third most expensive in the world. Mr. Mamdani said that is because “greed is baked into a lot of this economy.” He portrays capitalist profit incentives as a motive for firms to exploit workers, reduce the quality of goods and break the law.

Still, profit and wealth are not social defects to be discouraged; quite the contrary. In competitive markets, signals indicate that entrepreneurs have found ways to provide goods and services that consumers value. These incentives encourage businesses to innovate, produce more, reduce costs and discover better ways to meet people’s needs.

This must be a foreign concept to Mr. Mamdani, who believes that it is the government’s duty to provide the public with everything, from rent to groceries. He ignores commonsense solutions that have worked the world over, such as tax cuts and deregulation—and deportations, for that matter, which would reduce costs for households and businesses alike.

>>> Mamdani Is about to Make Housing Even More Expensive

Instead, Mr. Mamdani turns to central planning, even though government bureaucrats created many of the affordability problems he now insists they will solve.

Take housing. Mr. Mamdani argues that housing costs are central to New York’s economic problems, and many economists agree. Yet the city’s affordability crisis results from decades of restrictive zoning, burdensome permit requirements, development constraints, rent regulation and political barriers that limit housing construction.

#7702. Lawyers’ AI use doesn’t justify slashing $115K fee award, appellate court says

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award. (Image from Shutterstock)

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award.

Reuters reported Monday that the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver upheld a $115,000 fee awarded to defense lawyers at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck by the lower court in a trade secrets dispute. The trial court had ruled that the fee was reasonable.

“Plaintiffs have not shown that defense counsel’s use of AI rendered the hours that ​they actually expended unreasonable,” wrote 10th Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh for a unanimous three-judge panel.

The appeals court also upheld the ​dismissal of the lawsuit.

In her opinion, McHugh acknowledged that AI and similar research tools can make attorneys more efficient. But she stressed that lawyers must still verify legal authorities and arguments themselves.

According to Reuters, the case began in 2024, when industrial motor-efficiency equipment maker Flux Drive filed a suit against a Chinese manufacturer, alleging that one of its former engineers had stolen proprietary information and given it to them. After the case was dismissed, Flux Drive was ordered to pay the defendants’ legal fees. On appeal, the company argued that the defense billed for “ministerial tasks,” and that AI use should have lowered the bill.

The defendants countered that their lawyers checked every piece of AI-assisted research, and that Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated entry, redundant task or unreasonable charge.

Brownstein Hyatt partner Christopher Ottele, who represented the defendants, called AI a powerful tool that sophisticated firms should embrace.

“This ​decision confirms that the use of AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still ​must exercise in every filing with the court,” Ottele told Reuters.

Counsel for the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

#7701. Crime Is Down: Why Leadership Matters

For years, Americans were told by the left that rising crime was either exaggerated, the result of poverty, caused by COVID, or simply the unavoidable cost of modern life. None of those assertions is true.

Victims, police officers, prosecutors, and families living in high-crime neighborhoods knew better. They understood that crime is not an abstraction. It is a stolen vehicle, a broken window, a family traumatized by violence, or a neighborhood slowly surrendered to fear.

That is why the preliminary results of the just-released 2025 National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) deserve serious attention. The numbers point in one direction: crime fell substantially across nearly every major category measured by the survey.

The results are preliminary, and responsible observers will await final estimates and additional analysis. But the trend is unmistakable—and it coincides with a national agenda that has placed public safety, border security, law enforcement, and support for victims at the center of federal policy.

According to the preliminary estimates from the Bureau of Justice Statistics, the rate of serious violent victimization—violent crime excluding simple assault—fell 25%, from 9.9 victimizations per 1,000 people age 12 or older in 2024 to 7.4 per 1,000 in 2025. Aggravated assault declined even more sharply, dropping 31% from 4.5 to 3.1 per 1,000.

>>> Americans Lost Over $20 Billion to One Type of Crime. Here’s How We Can Fight It

The property-crime figures are equally striking. Property victimization declined 19%, from 138.0 per 1,000 households to 111.2 per 1,000. Burglary or trespassing fell 25%. Motor vehicle theft declined 30%, representing approximately 349,000 fewer stolen vehicles. Other household theft declined 19%, while burglary and trespassing represented roughly 460,000 fewer victimizations.

These are not minor statistical adjustments. They represent fewer people harmed, fewer families disrupted, and fewer communities forced to absorb the economic and emotional costs of crime.

The NCVS is particularly important because it captures criminal victimization whether or not the victim reported the offense to police. Each year, the Bureau of Justice Statistics gathers information from a nationally representative sample of approximately 240,000 people age 12 or older in about 150,000 households.

It therefore complements the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting data, which are based primarily on information supplied by law enforcement agencies.

The two measures tell a consistent story. The FBI’s 2025 data showed the largest year-to-year decline in violent crime since the agency began tracking national crime trends in 1936. Murder and non-negligent manslaughter declined by an estimated 18.1%.

The NCVS now provides an important second measure, reflecting the experiences of victims themselves.

What explains the decline? No serious analyst should pretend that a single policy produces every change in national crime. Crime rates are influenced by many factors, including local policing strategies, prosecution decisions, economic conditions, demographics, and community involvement. Preliminary survey results also cannot establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship.

But policy choices matter. A president who makes securing the border a priority, removes violent illegal aliens who are subject to deportation, directs the Justice Department to cooperate with the nation’s approximately 18,000 police departments, 3,400 sheriffs’ offices, and 2,300 elected district attorneys, funds law enforcement, and supports victims is sending a clear message: the government’s first responsibility is to protect the innocent.

>>> Another Win for the Task Force To Eliminate Fraud

That message matters. Criminals should expect enforcement, not indulgence. Police officers should know that federal officials recognize the risks they face. Prosecutors should have the resources and cooperation necessary to hold dangerous offenders accountable. Victims should not be treated as an afterthought in a system more concerned with the comfort of defendants than the security of communities.

“This report is proof that President Trump’s ’Make America Safe Again’ agenda is working,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said, the No. 3 official in the Justice Department.

The statement captures the broader significance of the data, even if conclusions should await final estimates: public safety improves when government treats it as a core mission rather than a campaign slogan.

The lesson is straightforward. Effective enforcement, cooperation among federal, state, and local authorities, secure borders, adequately funded police departments, and meaningful support for victims are not outdated ideas. They are practical necessities.

Americans should celebrate these preliminary gains while remaining vigilant. The goal is not merely to report that crime has fallen. The goal is to ensure that it stays down—and that every community, regardless of size or location, receives the protection its residents deserve.

#7696. The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

For years, the Left assumed Gen Z would be its most loyal supporters. Young Americans were expected to embrace socialism, distrust our institutions, and see government as the answer to the challenges facing our generation. But that assumption is increasingly being challenged by young people questioning the Left’s worldview and rediscovering the principles that made America exceptional.

The Left’s response has been revealing. Rather than defend its ideas, some of its most prominent voices are threatening the young Americans who dare to oppose them.

Recent remarks by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) offer a particularly alarming example.

Speaking about holding Trump administration officials accountable, Slotkin described using corruption cases to deter young Americans from joining the administration. She said she wanted prospective employees to worry that serving the Trump administration could mean buying themselves “a ton of problems.” Her stated goal was to discourage young people from getting involved.

Consider what that means for young Americans who want to serve their country by working for an administration, organization, or cause they believe in. The message is that choosing to build a career in the conservative movement could put a target on your back when the opposing side regains power.

>>> Dear Gen Z: Reagan Is Not a Relic

What an abhorrent message. Young Americans should be free to stand up for their convictions and pursue public service without fearing that their political affiliations could make them targets of the Left’s lawfare.

There is a world of difference between prosecuting actual criminal conduct and using the threat of prosecution to discourage participation in the political process. The justice system exists to enforce the law, not to intimidate political opponents or make an example of people whose political affiliations dissent from those in power.

Slotkin may frame her proposal as accountability. But when the stated objective is to deter young Americans from serving their nation, the question is whether the pursuit of justice is being conflated with the pursuit of political power.

Young Americans should find that deeply troubling, regardless of their political affiliation. And for a generation already questioning the Left’s vision for America, these remarks should prompt an even more fundamental question: Why should young people trust a political movement that seems willing to threaten their futures when they reject its ideas?

For years, the Left has presented socialism as a compassionate alternative to America’s founding principles. It promises equality through government control, security through dependence on the state, and progress through the expansion of political power. But beneath those promises lies a fundamental disagreement about human nature, individual liberty, and the proper role of government.

The American experiment rests on a different premise: that our rights come from our Creator, not the government, and that individuals—not political elites—should have the freedom to direct their own lives. Free enterprise, limited government, individual responsibility, and strong families are not outdated obstacles to progress. They are essential to preserving a free and prosperous society.

Socialism asks Americans to place greater trust in government. The American tradition asks government to respect the freedom and dignity of its citizens. One concentrates power in political institutions; the other recognizes that power must be limited to protect individual liberty.

For Gen Z, this is more than an abstract ideological debate. It is a question of what kind of country we want them to inherit—and whether they will be free to shape its future. Will they embrace a system that increasingly looks to government to direct society, or defend a nation built on the belief that individuals should be free to pursue their own aspirations?

The growing willingness of young Americans to challenge the Left’s assumptions should be welcomed as a sign of a healthy republic. No generation is obligated to accept socialism simply because it is presented as compassionate or inevitable. Young Americans have every right to question the Left’s promises, reject its prescriptions, and choose a different path.

>>> The Cost of Growing Up: Why Gen Z Feels Priced Out of the American Dream

At The Heritage Foundation, I see why preparing the next generation to defend America’s founding principles matters. Those principles do not survive on their own. They depend on young Americans who understand what is at stake and are willing to stand up for individual liberty, free enterprise, and limited government—even when doing so puts them at odds with the prevailing political culture.

Conservatives must make that case with conviction. We must demonstrate why the American tradition offers a better vision than the Left’s growing faith in government power. We must also ensure young Americans have the confidence and knowledge to defend that vision on their campuses and in their communities.

But the Left must answer for its own conduct. If its ideas are so compelling, why respond to young Americans who reject them with threats of prosecution? If socialism offers a better future, why should its advocates fear a generation willing to challenge it?

Slotkin’s remarks expose the danger of a political movement that increasingly treats ideological opposition as something to suppress rather than an argument to win. The threat is not simply that young Americans may be discouraged from joining an administration. It is that political participation itself could become a source of fear when the wrong people hold power.

Gen Z does not owe the Left its allegiance, and no political movement has the right to intimidate young Americans into submission.

The future of the American experiment depends on a generation willing to think independently, reject failed ideologies, and defend the freedoms that make this country exceptional. If the Left cannot win that generation through its ideas, it has no business trying to scare it into silence.

#7695. Religious Liberty, Terrorist Ideology, and the Limits of School Choice

Last year, Texas enacted one of the country's most expansive school-choice policies. The Texas Education Freedom Accounts program now serves more than 100,000 students, enabling families to choose the learning environments that align with their values and best meet their children’s learning needs.

School choice at this scale is worth celebrating. School-choice policies reflect the Constitution’s commitment to religious liberty and America’s longstanding recognition that parents, not the state, are the primary educators of their children.

A century ago, the Supreme Court struck down a Ku Klux Klan-backed Oregon law that would have banned private schooling, ruling in Pierce v. Society of Sisters that “the child is not the mere creature of the state.” Parents, the Court recognized, have the right and primary authority “to direct the upbringing and education” of their children.

Half a century later, in Yoder v. Wisconsin, the Court reaffirmed the “fundamental interest of parents to guide the religious future and education of their children.” The Court declared that only “interests of the highest order” can override these fundamental freedoms.

The Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue (2020) and Carson v. Makin (2022) decisions built on that foundation, holding that states cannot exclude otherwise qualified private schools from generally available scholarship programs merely because they are religious. The Court ruled that such discrimination is “odious to the Constitution.”

But Texas policymakers are now facing a question that school-choice advocates cannot avoid: What if parents choose schools funded by foreign adversaries that indoctrinate students to hate people who are not like them, and whose founders and staff have documented ties to terrorist organizations?

>>> School Choice Is About Religious Liberty, Not Just Better Test Scores

What is the limit of school choice?

Earlier this year, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott drew a line when he declared: “There’s no school choice for schools with ties to organizations that have connections to terrorism.” Several months earlier, Abbott had designated the Muslim Brotherhood and the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) as foreign terrorist organizations. (CAIR is challenging that designation.)

After those designations, acting comptroller Kelly Hancock wrote to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton asking whether schools with ties to those organizations or the Chinese government could be excluded from the TEFA program. Paxton’s reply was unambiguous: “Let me be crystal clear: Texans’ tax dollars should never fund Islamic terrorists or America’s enemies.” Hancock then announced no schools with such ties would receive Texas tax dollars through TEFA.

That principle—that public funds should not flow to schools with ties to terrorist organizations or hostile foreign powers—is sound. All freedoms have limits. Liberty is not license. A state has a compelling interest in ensuring that taxpayer dollars do not subsidize the indoctrination of children to hate America or to support terrorism.

But even the soundest principle can be implemented in an unsound, or even unconstitutional manner.

In March 2026, Houston-area attorney and father Mehdi Cherkaoui filed a federal lawsuit against Paxton, Hancock, and Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath, alleging that state officials had “systematically targeted Islamic schools for exclusion based on their religious identity.” His complaint observed that as of early 2026, hundreds of private schools across Texas—including numerous Christian schools—had been approved for TEFA, while not a single accredited Islamic school had been admitted. Cherkaoui sought to use TEFA funds to cover his children’s tuition at the Houston Quran Academy, but the school was not approved under the program. Three Islamic schools and additional parents joined a second suit shortly thereafter.

State officials denied the discrimination charge, explaining to the court that the comptroller’s office “had issues with processing and reviewing schools accredited by the nonprofit Cognia, regardless of whether they have Islamic affiliations.”

U.S. District Judge Alfred H. Bennett was not satisfied with that explanation. On March 17, hours before the original application deadline, he issued a temporary restraining order. At the emergency hearing, Bennett called the complete absence of approved Islamic schools “troubling,” remarking: “If you were to roll dice in a game of chance… you would not come up with those numbers. The appearance of this reeks.” He extended the student application deadline to March 31 and ordered state officials to receive and process applications from Islamic schools through the normal TEFA process. Within days, four Islamic schools were admitted: Brighter Horizons Academy in Garland, Bayaan Academy, Excellence Academy near Plano, and the Houston Quran Academy.

If it is true that the Muslim schools were not approved solely due to their religious affiliation, that would be a clear violation of their First Amendment rights. The Constitution’s guarantee of religious liberty undoubtedly prohibits such blanket discrimination.

However, the story is not so clear-cut. Two of the four schools now receiving TEFA funds—Brighter Horizons and the Houston Quran Academy—are at the center of serious, documented concerns regarding their institutional histories and affiliations.

Brighter Horizons Academy, based in Garland, is a subsidiary of the Islamic Services Foundation. According to a detailed investigation by the Middle East Forum (MEF), the school was established in part by Rasmi Almallah, who served on the board of the Holy Land Foundation—the largest terrorism financing operation in American history—and was named an unindicted co-conspirator in its 2008 federal trial.

ISF’s 2001 tax filings listed Mufid Abdelqader, a convicted HLF official and the brother of senior Hamas leader Khaled Mishal, as vice-president. His niece, Sarah Abdulqader, is currently a teacher at Brighter Horizons, and MEF notes that she “has been a passionate supporter of her convicted Hamas-financing father.” Previous staff reportedly included ISF director Nabil Sadoun, the lead author of ISF textbooks used at Brighter Horizons, a Jordanian Islamist activist whom the Dallas Morning News reported was “deported from the United States in 2010 for concealing Hamas ties on immigration paperwork.”

Some content in those ISF textbooks, used at Brighter Horizons and numerous other Islamic schools, is deeply troubling. According to MEF, one textbook teaches children ages seven and eight that non-Muslims are “the worst of creatures.” Another stresses the importance of jihad [the war against non-believers], stating: “When Muslims gave up jihad, did not abide by God’s will, started fighting among themselves and were submissive in the face of their enemies, God caused them to suffer greatly by allowing them to be dominated by those who do not fear Him or have any mercy for Islam.” The textbooks praise figures listed as unindicted co-conspirators in the Holy Land Foundation terror financing trial, including one who “describes suicide bombers and Hamas terrorists as ‘freedom fighters’ and ‘martyrs.’”

The school’s foreign funding adds another dimension. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies reported that Brighter Horizons received approximately $995,000 from the Islamic Development Bank for construction and expansion. Iran, a U.S.-designated state sponsor of terrorism, holds a significant capital share in the Islamic Development Bank and has representation on its governing board. During the Second Intifada, the bank directly managed funds that were paid to families of Palestinian terrorists who had been killed, injured, or imprisoned.

The Houston Quran Academy is operated by the Muslim American Society’s Katy Center (MAS). Federal prosecutors have described MAS as “the overt arm of the Muslim Brotherhood in the United States.” The academy’s principal, Hamed Ghazali, also chairs MAS’s Council of Islamic Schools. In 1988, Ghazali appeared to solicit funds for organizations later found to have financed Hamas. The next year, he “openly defended calls for the killing of Salman Rushdie.” In 2019, members of Congress called for an investigation into a MAS Philadelphia branch after it hosted an event in which children sang about torturing and beheading Jews.

>>> Stop Writing Blank Checks to Campuses That Protect Hate

These are not isolated cases. Middle East Forum data counts almost 800 Islamic educational initiatives across the United States, of which a clear majority are under Islamist control. Ninety of these institutions are in Texas, and several dozen may benefit from the new school subsidy program. Across those schools, MEF investigators found staff members who have shared Hamas propaganda, praised convicted terrorists, called for the destruction of America, and had children pledge loyalty to the Iranian supreme leader. Much of this infrastructure is tied to foreign money and foreign movements.

These are investigative findings, not criminal convictions against the schools themselves. But they are serious enough that state officials were right to ask questions. The comptroller’s supposed initial approach—a blanket exclusion of all Islamic schools—collides with the Constitution’s guarantee of free exercise of religion. Judge Bennett was right to find that troubling. But a blanket approval driven by litigation is also troubling.

The solution to an overbroad exclusion is not a rubber stamp, but due diligence. States must comply with the Constitution while protecting against terrorism. That requires examining each applicant school on its own record. Some Islamic schools clearly should qualify for the TEFA program. Whether Brighter Horizons and the Houston Quran Academy belong there is a harder question, and one the state should be able to answer through genuine investigation rather than blanket exclusion or court-compelled approval.

States should provide families access to robust school-choice options while protecting religious liberty. State officials should also take their duty seriously to avoid funding schools with genuine ties to terrorism. Those goals are not mutually exclusive. They require only that officials be precise, consistent, and willing to do their homework.

#7694. Philadelphia Is Dusting Off the Subprime Playbook

Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker wants to make her city the first in the nation to offer a city-backed mortgage, available to people who wouldn’t otherwise qualify for a loan. If that sounds familiar, it’s because loosening lending standards was the recipe for the housing bubble of the early 2000s, and the City of Brotherly looks ready to bake that cake again.

Under the mayor’s One Philly Mortgage plan, first-time buyers with “less-than-perfect credit” could put down as little as 3 percent, pay no private mortgage insurance, and get an interest rate roughly 1 percentage point below market, while public funds cover part of the interest payments. If the loan goes bad, the city covers it, meaning taxpayers foot the bill.

And that bill could be quite large, judging by the mayor offering a credit score of 620 as an example of who the program will serve. That’s right on the line traditionally used to separate subprime borrowers. Lenders have good reason for preferring higher credit scores and eschewing subprime borrowers: lower scores are highly correlated with increased default risk.

Credit scores aren’t some kind of moral judgment but a statistical proxy for the likelihood that someone will repay a loan. They’re formed from decades of data across millions of loans, not opinions or feelings. Someone with a higher credit score is less likely to default on the same loan as someone with a lower score. 

Likewise, lenders use additional tools like verified income to establish whether a borrower can actually afford the proposed monthly payment, while a down payment shows the borrower has the discipline to save and gives him skin in the game. Additionally, it provides an equity cushion that protects both borrower and lender if home prices dip, which has happened in many markets over the last few years.

>>> U.S. Government-Backed Homebuying Market Drives Up House Prices for Ordinary Americans

But with the mayor’s proposed plan of only 3 percent down, that cushion is paper thin. Selling a home often costs 6 percent or more in commissions and closing costs, so a buyer with 3 percent equity is effectively underwater the day he moves in. If he loses his job or faces a big repair bill, he can’t sell his way out. That’s when defaults turn into foreclosures.

The nation already learned that lesson the hard way, but apparently Parker forgets that, in the early 2000s, Washington pushed hard to expand homeownership, and lenders relaxed their standards to oblige. Down payments shrank, credit requirements loosened, and “liar loans” that skipped income verification became commonplace.

By 2006, roughly one in five new mortgages was subprime. When interest rates rose and home prices stopped rising, the defaults came in waves, millions of families lost their homes, and taxpayers were left footing the bill for bailouts by the Treasury and Federal Reserve, most of which just benefited Wall Street.

Banks ordinarily underwrite loans carefully because they bear the risk of default. Even if they sell a loan, they get top dollar for it when the default risk is low, so there’s still an incentive to lend carefully. When government promises to cover losses, however, that prudence disappears.

Under Parker’s scheme, the banks get to collect interest, some of which is paid for by taxpayers, and then those lenders don’t have to worry about losses because taxpayers will cover those too if they arrive. It’s privatized profits and socialized losses—no wonder Citizens Bank wants to participate! That’s what made the last bubble so destructive, and it’s exactly what a loan loss reserve does.

The mayor may have the best of intentions, but there’s an infamous road constructed with those. And while supporters point to a Massachusetts program that is supposedly both similar and successful, that hasn’t been without costs to taxpayers either. Nor is it necessarily comparable to what Parker’s pursuing.

>>> How to Make Housing Affordable: Build More Homes

Massachusetts households earn far more than Philadelphia’s, and Philadelphia’s housing stock is older and more distressed. What works in Boston’s suburbs won’t necessarily work in Kensington—they’re fundamentally different markets.

Philadelphia has one of the highest poverty rates of any big city in America. Even Drexel economist Kevin Gillen warns that expanding homeownership through risky lending without addressing poverty and distressed housing could raise foreclosure rates, especially when buyers take on repairs they can’t afford.

It’s true that housing affordability has deteriorated badly in recent years, including in Philadelphia, where it now takes 47 percent of the median household’s pre-tax income to cover the monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced home. But that answer isn’t putting taxpayers on the hook for loans that private lenders would never make on their own.

Instead of creating a subprime bubble, the city could reduce property taxes and permitting delays or enact zoning reform to make building and living in Philadelphia more affordable. Unfortunately, cutting taxes or red tape doesn’t lend itself to a flashy interview for the mayor the way subsidizing irresponsible lending does. Besides, taxpayers won’t see the final bill for years.

#7693. Trial opens for suspect whose multiple email threats include ‘skinning’ federal judge

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.” (Image from Shutterstock)

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.”

David Brooks Pokorny, 45, of El Cerrito, California, allegedly sent 11 email threats in a span of 44 minutes to assault, kidnap and murder Breyer, a senior judge for the Northern District of California, according to U.S. Assistant Attorney Kent Stejskal in opening statements Tuesday.

“Words within those 11 emails constitute what are called true threats,” said Stejskal, according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

He allowed the 14-person jury to view snippets of the emails during the trial. Pokorny is charged with making felony threats against a judicial officer and faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

According to Pokorny’s public defender John Reichmuth, his client’s words were “truly shocking, truly offensive, truly ugly, but not true threats.”

Reichmuth said the emails were free speech, and the prosecution would have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Pokorny, who has a history of sending threats to public officials and media outlets, meant to perform the actions described in his emails.

Presiding U.S. District Judge Jon Tigar of the Northern District of California noted that the prosecution does not have to prove that Pokorny intended to carry out the threat for it to supersede the protections of First Amendment free speech rights.

#7692. Freedom Isn’t Automatic—Each Generation Must Fight To Keep It

President Ronald Reagan’s famous warning that “Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction; it has to be fought for and defended by each generation” is even more relevant today than when he first said it.

He correctly identified that prosperity is not a predetermined outcome. It is created and sustained by culture, institutions, and economic freedom, and it must therefore be the responsibility of every generation to protect and preserve it.

The comforting but misguided belief in economic determinism—holding that prosperity is determined by geography, natural resources, or historical circumstances—must be rejected. By this logic, the United States was destined to be a superpower simply because it occupies a resource-rich continent and is protected by two oceans.

Natural resources and geography may create opportunities, but they do not guarantee prosperity. History shows that Americans have intentionally pursued free enterprise, transparent institutions, and a limited federal government system that transformed opportunity into prosperity and allowed the nation to flourish.

The myth of economic determinism can be revealed by one of history’s most compelling natural experiments: North Korea and South Korea. The stark development trajectories between the two is evidence that political choices impact national outcomes. After World War II, North and South shared a common culture, language, geography, and history, yet chose dramatically different political and economic systems.

>>> The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

South Korea embraced free enterprise, international trade, and economic liberation. North Korea adopted central planning, state ownership, and authoritarian rule. One developed into one of the world’s most advanced economies with residents enjoying personal freedoms and prosperity, while the other remains impoverished and isolated.

This contrast is even visible from space. Satellite photographs show South Korea illuminated at night by extensive infrastructure and a vibrant city, while North Korea remains dark due to an undeveloped power grid, poor infrastructure, and political factors that prioritize military needs over civilian energy consumption.

Geography didn’t create that divergence—communist policies did.

Similarly, Venezuela was among the wealthiest nations in Latin America for much of the 20th century, driven by large oil reserves. If natural resources guaranteed prosperity, it would be among the richest countries today. Instead, Venezuela fell from one of the most prosperous South American countries to one of the least prosperous in the world, with the Fraser Institute’s Economic Freedom Index ranking Venezuela number 22nd globally in 1980 and number 165th in 2021.

In less than half a century, empty promises made by socialist policymakers and enacted big-government policies undermined Venezuela’s economic foundation. The Manhattan Institute finds three policies implemented by dictator Hugo Chavez responsible for the nation’s widespread economic and humanitarian crisis: “nationalization of private industry, currency and price controls, and the fiscally irresponsible expansion of welfare programs.”

Chavez first nationalized agriculture by taking wealth and property from landowners and giving it to workers—leading to mismanagement and destruction of those resources. He then implemented controls to keep prices artificially low, which pushed out remaining firms and led to nationalized central authority. Finally, he expanded welfare programs purported to address poverty, educational shortcomings, and healthcare; all financed through high taxation and currency printing to the point of hyperinflation.

Inflation spiked, shortages of food and medicine became commonplace, government dependence increased, investment collapsed, and millions emigrated out of the country in search of better opportunities.

>>> The Conservative Coalition We Need to Save the West

But remember, in 1998 Chavez was democratically elected president. He campaigned on providing relief to poor- and middle-class populations by redistributing oil wealth in the form of social services—awfully similar to the “tax the rich” slogans of American socialists today. What starts with government programs, free buses, and artificially lower grocery prices ends with centralized authority, overreach, and the very socialist regimes that have killed citizens and destroyed entire countries in practice.

The lesson is that prosperity depends on policy—and this fact is increasingly relevant in the United States.

Socialist ideology has already made its way to America’s blue cities, with the youth driving this ideological shift from capitalism to socialism. Their affordability grievances are real, yet history repeatedly demonstrates that concentrated power in the hands of the state risks liberty, innovation, and long-term prosperity.

America’s future is not guaranteed. It depends on whether future generations defend and renew the principles and economic systems that historically made America great. Individual freedoms, economic mobility, and national prosperity should not be considered expectations, but rather privileges of ordered policies and culture.

That’s why policymakers and citizens must constantly, intentionally agitate for limited and constitutional government, a strong rule of law, and free enterprise to secure America’s future—because as Reagan reminded us, economic destiny is not guaranteed. It’s fought for and won time and time again.
